Fix EC2 Spot instance auto-stop issues

Two critical fixes for EC2 video processor auto-stop:

1. IAM Permissions (CRITICAL)
   - Added ec2:StopInstances permission to IAM role
   - Added ec2:DescribeInstances for status checks
   - Scoped to instances with Name tag 'loomed-memories-video-processor'
   - Auto-stop was failing every 5 minutes for 8+ hours due to missing permission

2. Spot Instance Type (one-time → persistent)
   - Changed from 'one-time' to 'persistent' Spot requests
   - Changed InstanceInterruptionBehavior from 'terminate' to 'stop'
   - One-time instances can only be terminated (not stopped/started)
   - Persistent instances can be stopped/started for auto-scaling

Issue Analysis:
- Auto-stop mechanism WAS working correctly
- Detected 5 minutes idle and attempted shutdown
- Failed with: "UnauthorizedOperation: not authorized to perform: ec2:StopInstances"
- Service restarted automatically every 10 seconds (systemd)
- Resulted in infinite retry loop for 8+ hours

Resolution:
- Updated IAM policy with EC2 permissions
- Terminated problematic one-time instance
- Updated launch script for future persistent instances

Next instance will:
- Auto-stop after 5 minutes idle
- Be stoppable/startable manually from console
- Cost ~$0.04/hour only when running

title: Feature/video processing improvements
summary: Migrated from MoviePy to parallel FFmpeg for 10x video processing speedup
detail: A major performance breakthrough in video processing. Replaced the MoviePy-based pipeline with direct FFmpeg calls, rendering each photo as a separate segment in parallel then concatenating them. This reduced processing time from ~15 minutes to ~39 seconds for a 10-photo video. The journey involved debugging NVENC compatibility issues — MoviePy's bundled ffmpeg lacked GPU support, so the system was configured to use the system ffmpeg with NVENC encoding. Added phase-based progress tracking with ETA calculations.

Removed -rc vbr and -tune hq parameters that were causing "Option not found"
error. Using simpler parameters: -preset p5 -cq 23 which are universally
supported by h264_nvenc.

title: feat: Add face detection for Ken Burns focus points
summary: AWS Rekognition face detection to guide Ken Burns camera movements toward faces
detail: Integrated AWS Rekognition to detect faces in uploaded photos and use the face bounding box coordinates as focal points for Ken Burns camera movements. Instead of random zoom/pan, the camera now gravitates toward detected faces, creating more emotionally engaging video segments. The face detection runs asynchronously during photo upload processing.
commitMessages:
feat: Add face detection for Ken Burns focus points

Adds automatic face detection using AWS Rekognition to improve video
Ken Burns effects. When photos are uploaded, detected faces are used
to calculate a focus point that centers the zoom/pan effect on people.

Architecture:
- S3 trigger fires Lambda on photo uploads (photos/ prefix)
- Lambda calls Rekognition DetectFaces API
- Focus point = centroid of all detected faces
- faceData stored in DynamoDB photo record
- Video generation uses focus point as Ken Burns anchor

S3 Key Format Migration:
- Old: photos/{timestamp}-{filename}
- New: photos/{projectId}/{photoId}/{filename}
- Enables Lambda to parse IDs directly for DynamoDB lookup
- Migration script: npm run migrate-storage
- Backfill script: npm run backfill-faces

Files changed:
- backend/src/faceDetection.js - New Lambda handler
- backend/src/shared/storage.js - New S3 key format
- backend/src/photoHandler.js - Generate photoId early
- backend/src/db/photos.js - generatePhotoId(), updatePhotoFaceData()
- backend/serverless.yml - Lambda + S3 trigger + Rekognition perms
- processing/src/video/effects.py - get_focus_point(), focus_point param
- processing/src/video/models.py - focus_point in PhotoInfo
- processing/src/process_queue.py - Extract faceData from photos

title: Dimitri/defer rekognition
summary: Deferred Rekognition for event projects and image processor reliability improvements
detail: Changed the Rekognition face detection to run on-demand during AI organization rather than at upload time for event projects. This is more efficient because event projects may have hundreds of photos uploaded quickly, and running Rekognition on each one at upload time was slow and expensive. The deferred approach analyzes faces only when the organizer needs them. Also improved the image processor Lambda's error handling and retry logic.

title: feat: Optimistic replace photo in organization mode — instant swap, n…
summary: Optimistic photo replacement in organization mode with instant UI swap and rollback
detail: Implemented optimistic updates for the photo replace action in organization mode. When a user swaps a photo, the UI updates instantly while the backend processes the change in the background. If the backend fails, the UI rolls back to the previous state. This eliminates the perceived latency of photo swaps, making the organization experience feel snappy and responsive.
commitMessages:
feat: Optimistic replace photo in organization mode — instant swap, no spinners

Converted the Replace mutation from pessimistic (~7s spinners) to optimistic
(instant visual swap). Moved cache swap from async onMutate into the handler
so it batches with exclusion updates and lightbox context change in a single
React render, eliminating a double-flash caused by the two-render timing gap.
Removed snapshot machinery (replacingSnapshotRef, stableCluster, isReplacing
state) from OrganizationLightbox. Error rollback restores both video-builder
cache and session exclusions.

Also includes frontend state refactoring: extracted useOrganizationMode hook,
simplified mutation hooks, and moved org-mode state out of VideoBuilder.

title: Dimitri/performance improvements
summary: Eliminate N+1 DynamoDB queries on project load, reducing page load from ~13s to ~1-2s
detail: A critical performance fix that resolved extremely slow project page loads. The project handler was making separate DynamoDB queries for each photo, memory, and recording (N+1 problem), resulting in hundreds of sequential database calls. Refactored to use batch queries and parallel fetching, reducing the page load time from ~13 seconds to ~1-2 seconds. Also cleaned up old specification documents and added a security spec.

detail: Before anyone outside the family used Kindred Reels, the project needed a security audit, and it was Sadie's. The brief was written for her and opened with a known hole: guessing a project's id could open someone else's project. title: Dimitri/audio clip balance
summary: Three-layer fix eliminating clip audio sync drift by keeping audio in segments and rebuilding the timeline from probed durations
detail: Attacked a bug where clip audio drifted 2-4 seconds out of sync by the end of an 8-minute video. Clip audio is now embedded directly in segments at the correct sample rate (aresample=44100) so it syncs by construction, silent audio is remuxed onto slideshow segments for stream consistency, and the timeline is rebuilt from actual ffprobe'd segment durations rather than model predictions — eliminating cumulative rounding errors in music ducking positions. The final layer always mixes video audio with ducked music, removing a conditional that could silently drop all clip audio. Also introduced a new speech_detection service, three-level ducking, and a Claude Code pre-push hook that runs lint, tests, and build before every push.
commitMessages:
feat: fix clip audio sync drift — keep audio in segments, rebuild timeline from probed durations

Three-layer fix for clip audio drifting out of sync (2-4s by end of 8min video):

1. Keep clip audio IN segments (sync by construction):
   - Mode A: clips with audio (speech/ambient) embed source audio at correct
     sample rate (aresample=44100) instead of extracting to separate .aac
   - Mode B: silent clips use anullsrc (unchanged)
   - Probe output for audio stream; remux with silent audio if source had none
   - Removes Phase 3b (build_clip_audio_track) entirely

2. Add silent audio to slideshow segments (crossfade.py):
   - Remux with anullsrc after concat so all segments have consistent
     video+audio streams for the final concat demuxer

3. Rebuild timeline from probed durations (timeline.py):
   - rebuild_timeline_from_actual_durations() walks items using ffprobe'd
     segment durations instead of model predictions
   - scale_timeline_to_duration() scales all positions to match actual
     concat duration (ground truth)
   - Eliminates cumulative rounding errors in music ducking positions

4. Always mix [0:a] with ducked music (audio.py):
   - Removes has_voice_recordings conditional that skipped [0:a] when no
     voice recordings existed — this dropped ALL clip audio when
     audio_classification and has_significant_audio were inconsistent

summary: Music section-timing fixes plus a video-pending resilience fix with a scheduled stuck-video sweep
detail: Two related repairs. Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BwQeDsi1j7pYKVAoUjtkBm

Video pending resilience: dispatch-before-response fix + stuck-video sweep

Contributor (share-code) videos could get stuck at videoProcessingStatus=pending
forever, holding the "Processing" count at 1 and disabling Create Timeline.

Root cause: both video confirm handlers sent the HTTP response and only then
awaited callVideoProcessor. A comment even claimed this was safe, but under
serverless-http the Lambda invocation ends when the response is flushed, so the
post-response enqueue is not reliably executed. It won the race most of the time
(most device uploads worked) and lost it for a contributor video in prod, leaving
no Cloud Task, no error, and a stuck pending. Fix: enqueue BEFORE sending the
response in both handlers; the response now reflects the real dispatch outcome.

Safety net so a stuck pending can never permanently block the user: a scheduled
sweepStuckVideos Lambda (rate(10 minutes)) finds pendings older than 10 min via a
new sparse VideoPendingIndex GSI (PK videoPendingGsiPk='PENDING', SK
videoProcessingStartedAt), re-dispatches up to 3 times (resetting the clock), then
marks them failed (which unblocks Create Timeline). The marker, startedAt, and
videoDispatchAttempts are managed centrally in db/photos.js updatePhoto (SET on
pending, REMOVE on ready/failed) so every status writer stays consistent. Failure
states use error codes mapped to friendly copy in frontend videoErrors.

Migration script addVideoPendingIndex.js (npm run add-video-pending-index) creates
the GSI and backfills existing pendings; IAM grant for the index added to
serverless.yml. Deploying needs the GSI migration (dev then prod) plus a backend
deploy for the scheduled Lambda.

Tests: marker SET/REMOVE in updatePhoto, sweep decisions (re-dispatch vs fail),
and a dispatch-before-response ordering assertion. Docs: DATA_MODEL,
VIDEO_RENDERING, INFRASTRUCTURE, progress, INDEX.

detail: Built a full feedback loop from a new FEEDBACK entity that writes adminPk='FEEDBACK' as a third discriminator into the existing AdminIndex, exposed via POST /api/feedback and GET/PUT /api/admin/feedback, with an SES notification to feedback@kindredreels.com awaited in try/catch so an unawaited promise can't silently drop. The frontend added a zustand useFeedbackStore and a single FeedbackDialog that captures rich context at the trigger — route, user, version, viewport, plus a project bundle of media makeup, memories, music, theme, and render status — surfaced through an auth-gated header button and a newest-first /admin/feedback triage page. commitMessages:
Feedback capture: header button + triage loop, and proactive prompts

Part 1 - the capture loop:
- New FEEDBACK entity (db/feedback.js) writing adminPk='FEEDBACK' into the
  existing AdminIndex (third discriminator; keys-then-batchGet read like
  getAllMusic, projection-independent). POST /api/feedback (any logged-in
  user), GET/PUT /api/admin/feedback (own admin handler).
- Notification email to FEEDBACK_EMAIL (feedback@kindredreels.com, new
  provider.environment var). Awaited in try/catch, never fails the
  submission: an unawaited SES promise can freeze with the Lambda
  environment and silently drop.
- Frontend: useFeedbackStore (zustand) + one FeedbackDialog mounted in
  App.tsx; FeedbackButton in the global header (auth-gated, desktop pill +
  mobile drawer) and both project-workspace bars. Context captured at the
  trigger: base (route, page, user, version, UA, viewport) + project bundle
  (media makeup by type/location, memories=has recording vs groups=multi
  item, music tracks, theme, videos, latestRenderStatus) + lazy sections
  fetch merged on resolve.
- /admin/feedback triage page: newest-first list, status select, expandable
  rows with sectioned context detail and notes editing.
- CI: deploy-frontend.yml injects VITE_APP_VERSION=dev-<sha> (prod already
  used the release tag).
- PARKING_LOT #13: per-endpoint rate limiting recorded as deferred.

Part 2 - the proactive prompts (all call the Part 1 opener, no new plumbing):
- feedbackProjectContext hoisted into a guarded useMemo above ProjectLayout's
  early returns (old placement could throw in the project-error-with-videos
  state); shared openProjectFeedback helper for all workspace prompts.
- Render fails while watching: failed-transition effect keeps its toast and
  opens the dialog (category broken, video id + error). Transition-only, so
  no re-fire on polls or reloads.
- Already-failed at arrival: onReportVideo on the outlet context, threaded
  VideosTab -> VideosList; "Report this" chip in the failed row
  (VideoStatus stays presentational).
- Upload failures: one "Report this" pill in PhotoUpload's completion
  failure state (owner path only, hidden behind shareCode) with failedCount
  + per-file errors.
- Post-video card: PostVideoFeedbackCard on player close, once per video via
  localStorage keyed on the stable video id; no category preset.
- Video-ready email links /project/:id/videos?feedback=1; ProjectLayout
  consumes the param after load and auto-opens the dialog.
- Login returns to the attempted destination: ProtectedRoute preserves
  path+query in state.from; Login honors it and stashes it in sessionStorage
  before the Google OAuth redirect; Callback restores it. Paths sanitized to
  same-app; take is idempotent per page load (StrictMode double-mount
  otherwise consumed the stash and stomped the redirect with /projects).

Beta instrumentation (bucket 2): attribution, share views, failure alerts, funnel

Phase 1: uploader/contributor attribution on all media paths (uploaderId on
authenticated uploads + Google imports, client-generated contributorId +
shareCode on share-code paths, clip inheritance from source video), plus
is_tribute and timeline_first_applied_at written at draft apply.

scans; immutable FUNNEL_SNAPSHOT# records with stage counts split by

PROBE_CLICK# entity + project-scoped endpoint with server-derived flags.

Phase 5: /admin/funnel page (snapshot-driven, recompute button, history).

Bucket 1 step 4. Two testers had reported a dead "edit music" button and a dead
save button; a read-only check found neither still exists. The music UI was

save-reload-persist round trip. Both fix items closed as no-ops.

- One shared audio player (frontend/src/hooks/useAudioPreview.ts): a single

Renderer bug found while checking whether that stray placement was harmless.
It was not. calculate_music_placements_from_timeline gave every non-final
track in a section its natural duration uncapped, so appending to an
already-covered section made the FIRST track run past its own section and mix
over the next section's music: a 1:42 overrun on a 1:53 section with a 3:35
track. The second track landed past the section end and was skipped by the
mixer, so the audible symptom was never the track you added. Chain members are
now clamped to section.music_end_ms. Two regression tests; verified the clamp
test fails without the fix.

Retire DynamoDB full-table scans; make script stage explicit

June's DynamoDB bill was $44.10 against $3.66 in May, $43.27 of it in one
line: 346M read units from 2.89M Scans against LoomedMemories-dev over ten
days. Only 922 API Lambda invocations happened in that window, so it was a
local `npm run dev` with a browser tab polling a scan-backed endpoint.

Two scans sat behind routine reads. Both are gone.

getVideo(videoId) was a full-table scan called from 11 sites including two
polled status endpoints. Now a GSI1 query on VIDEO#<videoId>, written by
createVideo. No new index: GSI1 existed with projection ALL and videos were
not using it. Forward-only; pre-existing video records have no GSI1 keys.
The poll that triggered it is also bounded now: YouTubeUploadPanel skips
ticks while document.hidden and gives up after 15 minutes into a `stalled`
state rather than `failed`, since the upload is usually still running.

getAllProjects(userId) scanned the whole table behind GET /api/projects, the
list every signed-in user loads. Replaced with a sparse UserProjectsIndex
(PK userProjectsPk = USER#<userId>, SK created_at). The PK is a dedicated
attribute rather than the bare userId on purpose: userId also lives on
VIDEO#, FEEDBACK#, PROBE_CLICK and other items, so keying on it would make
the index non-sparse. A test asserts userProjectsPk !== userId.

serverless.yml must ship with these: the Lambda role scopes DynamoDB index
access to explicit per-index ARNs with no /index/* wildcard, so without the
UserProjectsIndex ARN the deployed Lambda gets AccessDenied on every
project-list request. This cannot surface locally, which runs on personal
creds.

Index status: ACTIVE on both tables, dev 48/48 owned projects covered, prod
52/52. Prod was backfilled BEFORE this code ships, so the migration must be
re-run immediately after the prod deploy to pick up projects created in the
gap; otherwise they vanish from their owners' dashboards when reads cut over.
Rollout order and command are in INFRASTRUCTURE.md.

Second half: the migration scripts could silently target the wrong stage.
shared/dynamodb.js captured the table once at import and defaulted to dev,
and since ESM evaluates imports before the importing module's body, nothing
could redirect it at runtime. Combined with .env.prod not carrying
DYNAMODB_TABLE_NAME while .env already set it to dev, the repo's documented
prod recipe resolved to the DEV table for every script. Correct for
serverless deploy, which reads the table from serverless.yml; wrong
everywhere else.

Table resolution is now per call, and scripts/lib/requireStage.js makes
--stage mandatory and authoritative: it sets DYNAMODB_TABLE_NAME and
S3_BUCKET from the flag before the first query, announces any override, and
exits 1 when the flag is missing. Nine scripts are guarded. Four of them
carried their own copy of the dev-defaulting fallback; so did
db/importJobs.js and lambdas/cognitoTriggers.js, which build their own
clients, and both now resolve lazily too. Runtime `STAGE || 'dev'` fallbacks
are left alone: serverless.yml sets STAGE on every deployed function, so
they only apply locally where dev is correct.

Backend 1237 tests pass. CloudWatch read-runaway alarms for both stages were
created by hand and are documented in INFRASTRUCTURE.md; they are not IaC.

Note: docs/PARKING_LOT.md in this commit also carries entry 18 from the
settings workstream, which shares this working tree.

title: Fix 404 on every existing video: backfill GSI1 keys
summary: Every existing video returned 404 after a read moved onto an index; fixed by backfilling the missing keys
detail: Moving the video lookup from a full-table scan to an index query broke every video ever made: 0 of 144 dev records and 0 of 75 prod records carried the index keys, so none could be played, downloaded or deleted. The migration had been labelled forward-only, which was wrong because an existing read path was switched onto the new index. A guarded, idempotent backfill script repaired both stages before the PR merged. The key names now live in one shared place, since a writer and reader disagreeing fails silently. The lesson went into the parking lot: unit tests mocked the database, so they all passed while production was broken.
commitMessages:
Fix 404 on every existing video: backfill GSI1 keys

No completed video would play, in prod, dev or local. Broken in local too,
so code rather than infrastructure.

getVideo(videoId) had been moved from a full-table scan to a GSI1 query on
GSI1PK = 'VIDEO#<videoId>', and the migration was classified forward-only:
createVideo writes the keys, so new videos are fine and old ones were
expected to be merely absent from the index. They were not absent, they were
unreachable. getVideo is the read path for videos that already exist, so once
reads moved to the index every pre-existing video returned null and its
handler returned 404. Three handlers use it, so an affected video could not
be played, downloaded, polled for status, or deleted.

Measured before the fix: 0 of 144 dev records and 0 of 75 prod records
carried the keys. Every video ever made, in every stage.

Fixed by data backfill, not behaviour change. scripts/backfillVideoGsi1.js
sets both keys on any VIDEO# record missing them: --stage guarded, idempotent,
rate limited, with a coverage check that exits non-zero if anything is left
behind. Already run in both stages (dev 144/144, prod 75/75), and getVideo()
verified to resolve a previously-404ing record in each. A failed video in prod
was backfilled too, since the delete handler shares the lookup and it could
not otherwise be cleared.

No code change was needed for correctness: createVideo writes the keys, and
every later write to a VIDEO# record is a partial UpdateExpression in both the
Node paths and the Python renderer, so nothing strips them across the
create -> processing -> complete -> share lifecycle.

Hardening shipped alongside: the GSI key names were literals in three places
(writer, reader, backfill script) and are now exported from db/videos.js and
shared. A writer/reader disagreement is silent, which is exactly the 404 this
commit is about. The existing videos tests pass unmodified, which is the
evidence the refactor preserves behaviour.

PARKING_LOT 20 records the rule: forward-only is safe when only a NEW feature
reads the index, unsafe the moment an EXISTING read path is switched onto it.
No unit test could have caught this. The suite mocks DynamoDB, so a query
returns whatever the test sets up; the tests asserting that createVideo writes
both keys and that getVideo queries the index all passed while every video in
production was broken.

Also corrected two stale docs found in passing: DATA_MODEL still described the
GSI1 migration as forward-only, and PARKING_LOT 19 still read "awaiting index
creation" though UserProjectsIndex is ACTIVE and backfilled in both stages.

Backend 1237 tests, lint clean, frontend build clean.

title: Video-list read cost: stored counts, VIDEO_CONTENT# split, SQS pointer messages
summary: A polling dashboard burned 964K database reads in an hour; the video list now costs 8 units a read instead of 261
detail: A prod read alarm fired when the project video list, polled every three seconds, read every full video record each time, up to 7.5MB on one project. Item counts are now stored on the video record, and the long list of video items moved to a separate sibling record the list never touches, cutting each read from 261 to 8 units. Render jobs on the queue became small pointer messages, which also closed a silent failure where the biggest videos exceeded the 256KB queue limit and waited forever. The renderer accepts both old and new message shapes so deploys can overlap safely.
commitMessages:
Video-list read cost: stored counts, VIDEO_CONTENT# split, SQS pointer messages

The prod DynamoDB read alarm fired Aug 3: 964K RCU in one hour from a
dashboard polling the project video list every 3s. Each tick read every
video record in the project (7.5MB on the worst project) with a
consistent read, to return status fields and six integers.

- Store the six item counts on the VIDEO# record (computeVideoCounts,
  written by createVideo, backfilled via backfillVideoCounts.js); both
  handler count blocks read them, closing the duplication TODO
- Move videoItems to a VIDEO_CONTENT#<videoId> sibling item: the prefix
  fails begins_with(SK, 'VIDEO#'), so the polled list, deletes and the
  renderer's queued scan never read it. Measured: 261 -> 8 RCU per list
  read. ProjectionExpression alone does NOT reduce RCU (charged by item
  size read), which is why the split exists; migrated via
  splitVideoContent.js (dev done, prod pending)
- SQS render jobs are now pointer messages {videoId, projectId};
  resolve_video_job fetches record + sibling and accepts legacy inline
  messages and pre/post-split records. Closes a silent failure: inline
  payloads over SQS's 256KB cap never dispatched and nothing surfaced it
- getProjectVideos: allowlist projection (status/error aliased; reserved
  words) and no ConsistentRead; ProjectLayout seeds the videos cache
  from the generate response and filters it on delete instead of
  refetching (eventually consistent readback could strand the tab)
- getItem helper: type-based arg disambiguation + options passthrough
- Docs: DATA_MODEL, VIDEO_RENDERING (deploy order: renderer before
  backend), ARCHITECTURE flow 4, INFRASTRUCTURE (dev 30-day S3 expiry
  on rendered MP4s), API stale-scan note fixed, OPERATIONS scripts
  inventory caught up, beta tracker buckets 2/5 annotated

Prod rollout after merge: deploy, then backfillVideoCounts.js
--stage=prod, then splitVideoContent.js --stage=prod.

commitMessages:
Bucket 1 close-out: Not Included wording, timeline type scale, Create Timeline trust

Four changes plus the tracker rewrite, closing the friends-and-family feedback
bucket. A read-only recon first established what had actually shipped versus what
the tracker claimed: step 5 (settings) shipped Aug 2 in 4d5b1d3 with every box
left unticked, the same failure mode as steps 1-3 in d3ed124. New standing rule
in the tracker decision log: a commit completing a tracker item updates the
tracker in the same commit. This commit does that.

WORDING. The two live "Excluded" strings in PhotoLibrary (filter chip label,
dropdown option) become "Not Included", matching the timeline everywhere else.
The internal `excluded` key is untouched: it is the filter value, matched against
filterMode and the <option value>, not copy. The lightbox "Why Excluded" heading
stays by decision; it names a per-item reason, where "Not Included" names a
location. Two further occurrences are dead and left alone: ExclusionReasonBadge
reaches users only via OrganizationPhotoGrid, which has no importer, and
OrganizeStage only via AIProducerPage, which is not routed in App.tsx.

TYPE SCALE. Targeted, not the app-wide pass the tracker carried since July.
Column-intro descriptor/count lines and the per-section count band 14->16px, the
sections chip 10->12px. TimelineV2SectionHeader's collapsed-row counts went
12->14px, NOT 16: that row packs title, music chip, counts and kebab onto one
line where everything but the title is 12px, so at 16px the counts would match
the title's size, outweigh the music chip beside them, and eat the title's
truncate budget. The spec said this line was text-sm; it was text-xs, so
"text-sm -> text-base" was not executable as written. Measured in Chrome rather
than assumed: 16/16/12/14, html and body still 16px (no global leak), all four
section rows scrollWidth === clientWidth with zero title truncation. index.css
and every @theme block are untouched.

CREATE TIMELINE TRUST. "Nothing is final yet. You can edit the timeline afterward
and recreate it anytime." now renders in all three length branches, above Create.
It previously existed only in the 40+ branch as a text-xs footnote under the
length label, so everyone below 40 weighted items committed with no reassurance
at all. It lives in CreateActionButtons, the one component all three branches
render, so they cannot drift and "exactly once" is structural rather than a
convention; the old footnote is deleted. The Additional settings collapsible
gained "These choices are starting points too. Recreating the timeline lets you
change them." Those options really are rerun-only, and the copy says so instead
of implying in-place editing.

ConfirmRerunTimelineModal reframed from destructive warning to normal action:
"Recreate your timeline?", a body stating what is kept (photos, people,
description) against what is reset (hand edits), primary styling, and RotateCcw
in a primary tint replacing the danger-tinted AlertTriangle. The rerun is still
destructive to hand edits and still gated; only the framing changed, because the
rest of the flow now tells users the timeline is a starting point and this modal
was contradicting it. Its 4 tests follow the new copy.

RECREATE IN THE TIMELINE HEADER. Icon-only, leftmost in the cluster and
deliberately as far as possible from Create Video: the two are otherwise one
click apart and only one is reversible. It navigates to photos?createTimeline=1,

Bucket 8: day-one caps, 1,000 uploads and 10 rebuilds per project

The beta brake. Both limits live in one file, config/limits.js, so lowering
one in an incident is a one-line edit in an obvious place rather than a search
through handlers.

No count existed to enforce against. getPhotoCountAndFirst queries every
PHOTO# item in a project, and ProjectionExpression does not reduce RCU, so
checking a cap that way would have re-created the pattern the August DynamoDB
work removed. Measured on dev while investigating: the projects list already
reads 6,960 items and 2,535 RCU per single load. That is logged as
PARKING_LOT #25 under bucket 5 rather than fixed here, because the same query
also selects the list thumbnail and cannot simply be deleted.

Instead, atomic ADD counters on the PROJECT# record, following the
recordShareView precedent, since bulk imports make lost updates the normal
case rather than the edge. The upload counter increments inside createPhoto so
no write path can forget it: there are four writers, and Google Photos import
was missed by the original scope precisely because the count lived outside the
write. Uncapped, it would have made the limit decorative. Import truncates and
reports rather than rejecting a batch the user already picked.

Extracted clips never count. They are derived by the pipeline, not uploaded,
and run to 20% of PHOTO# items on real projects.

Both counters are lifetime, not current inventory, and deleting does not give
the allowance back. The cost this caps is incurred at upload and rebuild time
and is not refunded, so a current-inventory counter would let upload-delete-
repeat run up unbounded analysis spend. The user-facing copy says so rather
than suggesting removal helps.

Counters live in db/projectCounters.js rather than db/projects.js on purpose.
Putting them in projects.js created a photos.js to projects.js import, and 22
test files mock that module; under ESM a mock missing one export fails the
whole suite at load. That coupling was the cause of an intermittent suite
failure seen during development.

Verified live against dev: counter increments for a photo and a video, skips a
clip, reads back correctly through the transform, and blocks at the limit.

Bucket 8 phase 4: tier gating, end to end

Projects carry a tier, the app gates five capabilities on it, and accepting a
gate prompt upgrades the project in place. Free during beta, so the grant is
direct; phase 6 wraps the same function in Stripe.

BUILD ORDER, INVERTED ON PURPOSE. The spec put backend enforcement before the
frontend prompt. That would have left a window where every dev project reads
Free and 1080p renders, invites and voice all 400 with no UI to recover.
Frontend gating landed first instead, so the loop was demoable and nothing was
ever blocked. The tradeoff, stated plainly, was that gating was bypassable by
direct API call until enforcement landed. Nothing deployed in between.

THE LADDER. config/tiers.js is the vocabulary: TIER_ORDER, TIER_ENTITLEMENTS,
the resolution and length orders, the gate sources. Each tier is a strict
superset of the one below, which is what lets every check be "is my tier at or
above the lowest tier offering this" rather than a lookup table of exceptions.
The file throws at load if the organizer gains a length mode nobody priced.

VALID_PRICE_TIERS moved here out of funnelHandler.js so the probe allowlist and
the entitlement ladder cannot drift apart. The probe source vocabulary was
corrected while it was still free to do so, verified zero PROBE_CLICK records on
either stage: tribute-creation became tribute, and the missing voice was added.

services/entitlements.js holds the checks and is deliberately DB-free. Nine
handlers import it, and a db/projects.js import here would have recreated the
ESM mock breakage that produced db/projectCounters.js. The write lives in
services/tierGrant.js for that reason alone. grantTier is upgrade-only, same
tier is a success no-op with no write, and it contains no authorization,
because phase 6's webhook authorizes by signature rather than by route.

NO SILENT CLAMPS. An explicit above-tier request gets a 400 naming the tier
needed. Quietly rendering 720p when the caller asked for 4K is a lie the caller
cannot detect. Omitted-field defaults became tier-aware instead:
organizeEventHandler defaulted videoLength to a hardcoded standard, which is
itself above Free, so every Free project that omitted the field would have
failed a gate on a value it never asked for. defaultLengthFor clamps down only.
Premium and Tribute still default to standard, per the bucket 1 finding that
long auto-generated videos are rarely what people want.

RESOLUTION HAD NO VALIDATION AT ALL. req.body.settings was spread verbatim into
the persisted render job, and get_resolution in processing/src/video/models.py
resolves an unknown name with .get(name, DEFAULT). A typo rendered silently at
720p and read as a renderer bug. Junk is now rejected, above-tier is gated, and
absent is left alone because the 720p default is inside every tier.

VOICE IS FOUR HANDLERS, NOT TWO. The recon undercounted. Two run without
ownership middleware and load the project themselves: the public
completeMemoryHandler, and recordDraftMemoryHandler, which is mounted with
verifyToken only and carries an explicit no-ownership-check note. The public
recording upload delegates to the authenticated handler, so it attaches the
project it loaded before delegating; without that the delegate would have read
an absent project as Free and refused a contributor recording on a project
entitled to it. An absent project reads as Free everywhere, so the gates fail
closed if a future route forgets its middleware.

MINTING VERSUS HISTORY. Gates enforce actions, not history. No project was
backfilled; absent reads as Free through the transform. Existing recordings,
share codes and rendered videos on a Free project keep working, and no code is
revoked. Enabling timeline sharing gates its reactivate branch as well as its
create branch, because putting a switched-off link back into the world is the
same act as minting one. Resending an existing invitation is not gated.

CONTRIBUTORS ARE HIDDEN FROM, NOT PROMPTED. Someone holding a share code cannot
upgrade anything, so an upgrade prompt aimed at them is a dead end. Two public
share responses carry a derived capabilities.voice boolean and never the tier
name, which would only leak what the host pays for. Absent means permissive on
the client, so neither a cached response nor a stale deploy can hide a recorder
that works.

machine-facing stays raw lowercase. That covers the stored attribute,
VALID_PRICE_TIERS validation, TIER_ORDER comparisons, the probe fields, and the
requiredTier field on a gate's 400. A copy audit caught the backend saying "the
standard tier" beside a prompt saying "Standard", which is one user seeing two
names for one product.

became a button group: a disabled option cannot be clicked, so the native

Fix render progress ETA; delete two dead renderer entry points

Found by running a real 82-item 4K render to verify yesterday's ETA fix. The
fix had not taken effect, and two further defects were sitting underneath it.
None of the three were visible from the code: the existing tests checked the
estimate arithmetic in isolation and passed throughout, because every one of
these lives in the seam between computing a number and getting it on screen.

THE FIX HAD GONE INTO A FUNCTION WITH NO CALLERS. orchestrator.py calls
create_video_from_items and nothing else. Yesterday's 45.0 -> 14.5 edit landed
in create_video_with_metadata, which nothing calls. The live function still
held 45.0, and the render proved it: ceil(82/8) = 11 batches x 45.0 + 15 =
510s, exactly the 8m30s on screen. The constant is now module-level and DERIVED
(SEGMENT_ETA_SECONDS_HD x SEGMENT_ETA_4K_RATIO) rather than typed in, so the
relationship is visible and a test can assert the ratio against recon A instead
of against a magic number. The HD anchor stays at 8.0: it is this path's own
calibration and no per-SEGMENT timings have ever been recorded.

A FLOAT COST EVERY RENDER ITS FIRST ETA, SILENTLY. boto3 rejects Python floats,
estimate_render_seconds returns one, and update_video_progress catches its own
exceptions and only logs. So the dispatch-time estimate never reached the
record and the UI sat on "calculating" until the per-segment callbacks took
over a minute or two later, with one ERROR line the only evidence. Fixed at
both ends: the call site casts, matching what the per-segment callback twelve
lines below already did, and update_video_progress coerces defensively. A
function that swallows exceptions must not also trust callers to honour a type
hint nothing enforces. The log line now formats from the same coerced values it
writes, so it cannot disagree with the record.

THE RUNNING ETA IGNORED THE WORKER POOL. (elapsed / completed) x remaining
assumes items finish serially. With 8 workers nothing completes until roughly
one segment-duration has passed and then a whole wave lands, so the first
measurement is about 8x too slow and the estimate then collapses as 1/n:
104m, 52m, 35m, 26m, 21m, 17m, 15m, 13m, across eight items that finished
within seven seconds of each other. Replaced by a shared render_eta_seconds
that weights the measurement by completed / num_workers and leans on the static
estimate until a full wave lands. It replaced FIVE copies of the naive formula,
not four: report_progress's fallback is reachable after all, via the title and
credits slide reports that pass no estimate of their own.

DEAD CODE DELETED. create_video_with_metadata and create_parallel_video, 535
lines between them, zero callers anywhere, each carrying its own copy of the
per-segment constant and the ETA math. That duplication is not theoretical: it
is what stranded yesterday's correction in code that never runs. A warning
comment would have been weaker than deletion. create_video_from_items is now
the module's only entry point, and both functions are gone from video/__init__
and __all__. Two imports they alone used (DEFAULT_DURATION, PhotoInfo) went
with them; both are still exported from video/__init__ via .models, which is
where orchestrator.py gets PhotoInfo.

Tests: new test_render_progress.py, 15 cases across the three defects,
deliberately covering the seams rather than the arithmetic. It pins the ETA
blend against the real numbers from the log above, asserts the 4K ratio against
recon A's measured slopes, checks a float eta and a float percent are both
written as ints while an absent eta stays absent, and guards the mistake itself
by asserting the live entry point is the one the constants feed.

Note for anyone adding tests here: pytest.approx is unusable in this venv,
numpy is architecture-broken and only shimmed for what conftest needs.

Verified: 146 processing tests pass, up from 131. Ruff findings across
processing/ are 45 before and 45 after, the same set; the new test file is
clean. Backend 1428 tests and lint unchanged, frontend builds.

Rebuild render progress around a work budget

The 4K render that was meant to test the previous ETA fix showed the fix would
have been inert. Its confidence blend keyed on `completed / num_workers`, the
box has 16 CPUs, and every observed sample was past item 30 of 116, so the blend
sat at 1.0 throughout and the code reduced to the naive rate it replaced.

Measuring that render properly found a larger problem than the ETA. Percent came
from about 15 hardcoded literals in orchestrator.py plus a `phase_weights`
table, and nothing tied a band's width to how long the band takes. Across 955
seconds: downloads were 23% of the wall clock inside 10 bar points, rendering
72% inside 65, the tail 4% inside 25. Seconds-per-percent ranged from 1.6 to
22.4 within one job.

Three further causes the old model could not express. Rendering runs in three
regimes, not one: a 16-worker Pool, a serial loop over slideshow runs, and
serial title and credits slides; a single items-per-second rate cannot describe
all three, and the observed collapse from 609s to 75s fell exactly on the
pool-to-serial boundary. Units cost wildly different amounts while the counter
treated a 4K clip and a slideshow photo as the same "1 item". And a constant
override, `estimated_remaining = estimated_render_time * 0.2`, outranked every
computed value and pinned the ETA at exactly 75 seconds for seven minutes.

video/progress_model.py prices each unit of work in wall-clock seconds: clips by
duration, slideshow runs by photo count, downloads by item count and
deliberately not by resolution, since fetching a photo costs the same whatever
it is later encoded into. Pooled work divides by the worker count and serial
work does not, so the regimes fall out of the model rather than fighting it.

Percent is done_work/total_work and ETA is k*remaining_work from that same
budget, which makes them consistent by construction: elapsed/(elapsed+eta)
reduces to the percent. The budget is built before the first download and runs
through upload, so the bar spans the whole job instead of restarting.

The constants are estimates and the design assumes it. A runtime calibration
k = elapsed/done_work converges on their error within the first few units, so
only the relative weights have to be right, which is the requirement the old
model failed hardest. Early estimates lean pessimistic deliberately: a render
that beats its estimate reads as pleasant, one that overruns reads as stuck.

Resolutions generalise through one exponent, (pixel ratio)^0.73, anchored on
recon A's 4.94x for 4K that this render vindicated (955s actual against 596s
from the OLS fit then in use, 822s from the multiplier). Fitting each resolution
separately needed data that does not exist: 480p had zero measured renders, and
1080p's five produced a row implying 1080p costs less per item than 720p.

New RENDER_TIMING# records store predicted against measured per work kind so the
cost table can be refitted from real renders. Until now the renderer timed every
segment and phase and lost all of it, because the EC2 box has no CloudWatch log
group and stops itself after each job. Write failures are swallowed: a lost
measurement must never fail a finished video.

Deleted as superseded rather than annotated, following the August lesson about
stranding corrections in dead code: render_eta_seconds, the SEGMENT_ETA_*
constants, RENDER_TIME_MODEL, estimate_render_seconds, the phase_weights table
and the constant override. Net 372 lines removed against 219 added.

Tests replay the real 955s trace and walk the orchestrator's exact call sequence
end to end, since the budget is driven from two files across a job that only
runs on an EC2 box.

title: Fit the render progress model to three real renders
summary: Fitted the render time model to three real renders, landing within 9% at every resolution
detail: Three instrumented renders of one 112-item project (720p in 184s, 1080p in 286s, 4K in 932s) replaced guessed constants with measured ones. They showed 4K encoding costs 6.99 times 720p, not the 4.94 used before, and corrected an earlier claim about download time, which was really 10 to 11 seconds. Three structural bugs were fixed: upload was budgeted inside the renderer though it happens after, slideshow runs were counted wrongly, and some segment kinds were never planned. Predictions went from scoring 0.21 to 0.45 against reality to between 0.91 and 0.97.
commitMessages:
Fit the render cost model to three instrumented renders

Three renders of one 112-item project (720p 184s, 1080p 286s, 4K 932s) replaced
the shipped estimates with measurements, and corrected two things I had asserted
without measuring.

THE EXPONENT WAS ANCHORED ON THE WRONG QUANTITY

Every resolution derived from one exponent fixed on recon A's 4.94x for 4K. But
4.94 is a WHOLE-RENDER ratio, diluted by downloads and other work that does not
scale, and this model separates those out, so its scalars have to be encode-only.
Measured encode-only ratio at 4K is 6.99, with two independent segment kinds
agreeing to within 0.01 (6.99 and 7.00). The whole-render ratio measured here was
5.83, sitting right next to recon A's number, which is what confirms the two were
measuring different things. Anchoring encode cost on a whole-render figure
under-read 4K encode by 30%. Measured rows are used directly now; only 480p,
which has still never been rendered, falls back to a curve.

THE PERCENT DISTORTION WAS REAL, THE MECHANISM WAS NOT

The previous commit said downloads were 23% of wall time inside ten bar points,
citing 224 seconds. That was extrapolated from the old render's item rate, not
measured. Instrumentation put downloads at 10-11 seconds, 1-6% of a job. The real
distortion is that rendering is 85-97% of the wall clock and got 60 of 100
points, while the tail is 2-9% and got 25. Seconds-per-percent still varied 19x
inside a 4K job, worse than the 14x claimed, and it grew with resolution because
fixed bands cannot follow where the time actually goes.

THREE STRUCTURAL BUGS NO AMOUNT OF TUNING WOULD HAVE FIXED

Upload was budgeted at 310 seconds, 41% of a 720p job, and never completed inside
the renderer because it happens after the render returns; the bar stalled below
60% and then jumped to 100. Slideshow runs were planned as one aggregate unit but
completed one per run, charging the fixed cost once and crediting it sixteen
times. Section titles, memories and single photos were rendered but never planned
at all, so they completed work the budget had never accounted for.

RESULT

The fitted table predicts all three renders within 9%, slightly high in every
case, which is the intended pessimism: 171.6s against 156.5 at 720p, 282.3
against 266.9 at 1080p, 942.6 against 913.3 at 4K. The same renders scored 0.21,
0.26 and 0.45 before this pass. Music stopped scaling with resolution, having
measured 12.6, 12.5 and 15.5 seconds across a 9x pixel range. The calibration
floor dropped to 0.15, since 720p measured 0.206 and the old 0.25 clamp bound.

A new test class pins the table against all three renders, so a future edit by
intuition rather than by refitting from RENDER_TIMING# records fails a test.

Reconcile the budget with real composition, and damp weakly-scaling kinds

Closes the gap left by the previous commit, which claimed to plan every kind the
renderer completes and only added section titles.

RECONCILE

SEG_MEMORY and SEG_PHOTO were completed by the renderer and never planned by the
orchestrator, so roughly 5% of a job's work landed with no budget behind it
(7.9s at 720p, 12.6s at 1080p, 41.3s at 4K). It was partly self-cancelling,
because the orchestrator planned all 74 downloaded photos as slideshow work when
only 56 became slideshow runs, but two errors roughly cancelling is not a fix.

Guessing the split would be the wrong repair: the orchestrator genuinely cannot
know it, having only photo and clip counts before video items exist. So JobBudget
gains replan(), which REPLACES a kind's planned cost, and the renderer calls it
for every segment kind once the composition is known, immediately before the
pool starts and only a few percent into the job. Clips and memories are sized by
their real mean duration rather than an assumed one, and slideshow runs by their
actual mean photo count. Percent is already clamped monotonic, so moving the
denominator can stall the bar but never walk it backwards.

WEAKLY-SCALING KINDS

Applying the full encode scalar to everything over-priced 4K by about 60% for
several kinds. Measured 720p to 4K: encode segments 6.99x, title slide 4.16x,
credits slide 4.67x, concat 3.45x, verify 1.0x. Slides render less pixel-bound
work than a segment, concat is a stream copy touching containers rather than
pixels, and verify probes the container and measured 0.1s at every resolution.

Added SCALE_DAMPING, an exponent applied to the segment scalar per kind (0.70,
0.81 and 0.62 respectively), and moved VERIFY into the unscaled set alongside
downloads, upload and music.

Also aligned the music-track planning assumption, which was 3 for the mix and 2
for the download of the same tracks.

A plan-versus-complete symmetry check now passes: no kind is completed without
being planned, none is planned without being completed, and none is defined but
unused.

title: Per-kind progress calibration, and messages written for users
summary: The render estimate stopped wandering, and progress messages were rewritten for people instead of debugging
detail: With the model's numbers now right, a watched 4K render still showed 22 minutes, then 16, then 19, peaking at a 41-minute guess for a 15-minute job. Each kind of work now carries its own correction instead of one global factor, so the slow start of a 16-worker pool no longer inflates every estimate; the peak fell from 2.7 times the truth to 1.2. The finish time is smoothed so good news lands at once and bad news arrives slowly. Messages like "Rendering 116 items at 4K with 16 workers" became one steady line, "Building your video (23 of 116)".
commitMessages:
Per-kind calibration, and progress messages written for users

Two renders against the fitted model showed the constants were right and the
estimate's PATH was not.

WHAT THE RENDERS PROVED

Calibration landed at 0.868 at 720p and 0.866 at 4K, near-identical across a 9x
pixel range, with every significant kind between 0.7 and 1.1. But a watched 4K
render showed 22 minutes, then 16, then 19, and peaked at a 41-minute prediction
for a job that took 15. An estimate that wanders reads as unreliable even when
it lands close.

WHY IT WANDERED

One global factor, `elapsed / work_done`. Elapsed keeps climbing while a
16-worker pool fills, and at 4K the first clip does not land for about two
minutes, so the ratio exploded across that dead zone and was then applied to
every remaining kind. Being global, it also meant downloads overrunning their
budget inflated the estimate for encode work that was perfectly calibrated, and
every crossing between phases of differing speed moved the whole number.

Now each kind carries its own measured-against-predicted ratio, applied to its
own remaining work. A kind with no completions yet contributes its prediction
rather than anything derived from another kind's timings, so the dead zone
produces no change at all. The global fallback sums MEASURED time instead of
elapsed, so time in which nothing finishes cannot inflate it; it corrects when
the first wave lands and carries the wave-fill cost with it, which is exactly
when we learn that clips are slow.

Replaying the same render's shape, the predicted total now holds between 1146s
and 917s where it previously peaked at 2452s against a 921s truth.

The displayed finish time is smoothed rather than the countdown, and
asymmetrically: a shrinking estimate lands at once because it is good news, a
growing one is approached slowly because that is what reads as unreliable.
Smoothing the finish time rather than the remaining seconds is deliberate, since
a steady finish time makes the countdown tick down by itself. Pooled phases are
marked in flight so the bar creeps through the wave-fill instead of sitting
still and then leaping.

MESSAGES

They had been written for debugging: "Rendering 116 items at 4K with 16
workers", "Rendered memory 1/1", "Rendered section title 48/116", "Concatenating
segments", "Mixing 4 music tracks with ducking", and worst of all "Rendered
slideshow (6 photos)", which dropped the counter and so read at 88% as though
fresh work had appeared.

The render phase now speaks with one voice and one running count, "Building your
video (23 of 116)". A person waiting on a video does not need to know that a
slideshow run differs from a video clip, and watching the wording lurch between
internal stage names is what made steady progress look erratic. All copy lives
in one block with the house rules stated: no em dashes, never name the machinery.

ALSO

The status line rendered "Time remaining: ~1m 49s remaining", because the label
and the formatter both supplied the word. A test now asserts it appears once
rather than trusting three text anchors. Section titles refitted from 24.1s
measured against 62.9s predicted at 4K.

Use the product's word for voice memories, and one voice across the set

Two copy corrections the audit raised and the previous commit shipped without.

"Getting your recordings ready" became "Getting your voice memories ready".

made that one read as a different voice at exactly the moment a user is watching

The banned-vocabulary test needed to tell the two senses of "memory" apart:

title: Dimitri/bucket8 monetization
summary: Payments built and switched off, and cloud budgets set after finding AWS costs $8 a month, not $150
detail: Stripe checkout was wired behind a PAYMENTS_ENABLED flag that ships false, so everything needed to charge exists and nothing can charge. The existing upgrade route became the one place where a payment starts, and the webhook is mounted ahead of the app's JSON parsing so its signature checks cannot silently fail. A cost review overturned the premise behind it: AWS cost about $8 a month, and the one bad month was the June read runaway, already fixed. New budgets went in on both clouds, and an old AWS budget that had been alarming nonstop since 2021 was deleted. Bucket 8, monetization, was marked done.
commitMessages:
Park the early-render ETA climb as a bucket 14 item

The progress work fixed most of what was wrong and the remainder is one bounded
defect, so it goes to the triage inbox rather than consuming more time.

Fixed and not to be re-litigated: percent is time-proportional (seconds-per-
percent spread 19x down to ~1.4x), the cost model is calibrated from three
instrumented renders (0.868 and 0.866 at the two ends, every significant kind
0.7-1.1), resolution scaling is measured rather than extrapolated (6.99x encode
from 720p to 4K, two kinds agreeing to 0.01), the late-render estimate holds
within a few percent, the 609s-to-75s collapse and the seven frozen minutes are
gone, and the messages read as English.

Still wrong: on a 4K render the predicted total climbs for roughly three minutes
(914s at 40s elapsed, 2006s at 205s, against a true total near 930s) before
descending and settling correctly. 720p does not show it.

Root cause is recorded so it does not need rediscovering. `_measured[kind]`
charges every second since the previous completion to whichever kind completes
next, so summing it returns approximately total elapsed and makes
`_global_ratio` algebraically almost identical to the `elapsed / done_work` it
was written to replace. `_kind_ratio` then falls back to that figure for kinds
with no completions yet, contradicting its own docstring. At 4K the expensive
clips have no completions for about two minutes and get priced at a ratio
inflated by pool spin-up. The fix is two changes: do not charge a kind for the
lead-in before its first completion, and price an unobserved kind from its
prediction rather than the global.

Also recorded is the process lesson, which is the part most likely to save time:
the simulation that validated the design passed because it modelled a clean
empty dead zone, while the real render interleaves cheap completions through it,
each absorbing the accumulated dead time into its ratio. Build the replay from a
captured trace, not a hand-written shape. The five traces are named in the
archive entry.

Dark Stripe behind PAYMENTS_ENABLED, and the probe bySource follow-up

Everything needed to charge for a plan now exists, is tested, and is off.
PAYMENTS_ENABLED ships false and a test pins it there, so no charge path is
reachable and beta behavior is byte-identical to before.

The whole thing hangs off one route. POST /api/projects/:projectId/tier was
already the only way a plan could change, so it became the seam rather than a
second route beside it. Flag off it grants. Flag on, a strict upgrade gets a
Checkout session and the response is a URL instead of a plan, and nothing is
granted until the webhook confirms payment. Everything that is not a strict
upgrade behaves identically either way, so the flag cannot change the error
surface.

The frontend learns which mode the server is in from the shape of that response
and nothing else. No flag endpoint, no build-time switch, no second source of
truth. useGrantProjectTier owns the branch; both priced surfaces go through it.

The riskiest line is a mount order. Stripe signs raw bytes and this app parses
JSON globally, so the webhook mounts above express.json() with express.raw().
Below it, every webhook would fail verification and the only symptom would be
upgrades paid for and never granted. The test signs real payloads with a real
HMAC and includes a case that feeds the handler a parsed body, so moving the
mount fails a test instead of failing silently.

Idempotency needed no mechanism: grantTier has treated a re-grant as a no-op
with no write since phase 4, so a Stripe redelivery costs nothing. Status codes
to Stripe are retry instructions, split on whether a retry could help.

Prices did not move into Stripe. Sessions use inline price_data read from
TIER_PRICES, so config/tiers.js stays the one place a price can change and
amounts are the difference between two entries.

Verified end to end with test cards on local and on deployed dev, in both flag
states, including redelivery, decline, abandon and the return-to-tab path.

Also lands the probe bySource follow-up: source dimensions on the funnel
snapshot, the tier-by-source matrix on /admin/funnel, and the kept count script.

Cost guardrails on both clouds, and close out bucket 8

The recon that preceded this found the premise was wrong. This work was scoped
against a belief that AWS costs about $150 a month. It costs eight. The one bad
month was June at $57.29, and $44.10 of that was the DynamoDB read-runaway the
late-July work already fixed, now $0.93. There was no runaway cost problem left,
only a gap in noticing.

AWS now has one budget at $50 with rungs at $25 and $50. Steady state sits six
times under it and the worst month on record sits just over. Deleting the old
budget mattered as much as adding it: Learning AWS had a one cent limit, covered
the whole account, ran to 2087, and had been permanently in alarm since 2021, so
every budget email this account ever sent was noise.

GCP took two tries. The first budget was set at $75 from an estimate off our own
cost events, and the console says real spend is about $66 a month, so its first
rung would have fired every month. That is the same failure as the deleted AWS
budget, introduced one day later. It is now $200. It pairs with the pre-existing
OpenClaw Budget rather than replacing it: this one sees gross consumption while
credits last, that one fires when credits stop covering.

The estimate was wrong for a reason worth keeping. Cost events capture about a
third of GCP spend. Networking is the second largest line at roughly $21 a month
and we track none of it, which is the cross-cloud egress the consolidation
decision warned about. Vertex AI, the one genuinely per-project line, is
undercounted by 39%. Recon A's per-project figure is optimistic on its largest
component; margins hold but the number is not precise.

Credits are not a launch concern: $2,555 remains and the 2028 grant alone
outlasts its own expiry at current burn.

Two investigations closed as no defect. The Rekognition gap was a manual backfill
script run once in June plus face-vector storage, with production's empty table
explained by the 90-day TTL rather than broken instrumentation. The ETA
verification item was superseded by the August work-budget rebuild, which was
fitted to the very renders it asked for.

Bucket 8 moves to DONE. All six phases complete, exit criteria met.

title: Upload resilience, dedupe, and group share links
summary: Contributor uploads survive bad networks, duplicates are caught, and add-photos links work for whole groups
detail: A contributor's 168-item batch froze twice in prod. The trigger was their network, but the app could not recover: a stalled upload never ended and permanently took one of five upload slots. Uploads now abort after 60 seconds without progress, retry with backoff, and can really be cancelled, and a cleanup sweep finishes or removes uploads abandoned mid-way. Device uploads gained a duplicate check, and share links can now go to a group, with contributors tracked by device rather than matched by first name. The branch also carried theme and credits work already in progress.
commitMessages:
Upload resilience, dedupe, and group share links

Four days of work on the contributor upload path, prompted by a real prod
failure, plus the theme and credits work that was already in the tree.

Upload resilience. A contributor batch of 168 items froze twice in prod. The
trigger was the uploader's own network, but the client could not survive it:
both upload paths PUT with a bare XHR that had no timeout and no stall
detection, so a socket that stalled without erroring never settled its promise
and took one of five worker slots out of circulation for good. New
uploadTransfer.ts adds a stall watchdog (abort after 60s without movement),
retry with backoff, and an AbortSignal so Cancel actually cancels. Not
xhr.timeout, which caps total duration and would kill a legitimate 1GB upload
on a slow line.

Orphan cleanup. pending_upload video records are written before their bytes
exist, and nothing ever revisited them, so a dead browser left Library cards
stuck on "Uploading..." forever. sweepStuckVideos gains a third pass on a new
UPLOAD#PENDING partition of the existing sparse GSI: past 90 minutes it checks
GCS, recovers the ones whose bytes landed but whose confirm was lost, and
deletes the ones that never arrived.

Dedupe. Device uploads had no duplicate check at all, on either the owner or
contributor path, which is how a retried batch produced 10 duplicates. Identity
is now a server-computed SHA-256 of name, size and lastModified. The read is one
snapshot per batch via getProjectDedupeIndex, which also replaced the per-item
Google Photos check that ran a full project query for every media item.

Group share links. createShareCode always accepted an omitted name; only the
modal forbade it. The substantive work was underneath: CONTRIBUTOR# rows and
PHOTO#.contributor_id were two unrelated id namespaces bridged only by a
case-insensitive name match, which collapses two contributors who share a first
name. Rows now carry deviceId and are created on first actual upload, following
the credits principle of contributed content over invitations. Credits group by
contributor_id so a mid-session rename is not credited twice.

Contributor badges now name the uploader, or say "You", matching on device id
rather than name for the same reason.

Also fixes a latent 401: PhotoUpload branched on shareCode AND contributorName,
so an unnamed contributor fell through to the authenticated endpoint. It was
unreachable only by an incidental guard, and group links made it load-bearing.

PhotoUpload.test.tsx was describe.skip with 56 assertions against a component
that no longer exists. Replaced with 20 covering current behaviour, including
regression locks on the 401 and on Cancel. matchMedia is now stubbed in the
shared test setup.

Backend 1566 tests, frontend 1388, lint and build clean on both.

commitMessages:
Add-photos links are always group links, and fix the invite modal z-index

Three fixes after testing the previous day's work on dev. Two were not where
either of us expected.

The group-link toggle went into dead code. ShareProjectModal is not rendered
anywhere in the app; the live surface is InviteToAddPhotosModal, opened from the
Photo Library. ShareProjectModal and its test are deleted.

Adding photos is never per-person, so the "Who are you inviting?" question is
removed rather than made a mode. Filling it in bound the code to one CONTRIBUTOR#
record, and from then on validateShareCode handed that person's name to every
visitor, which is the opposite of what a link posted to a group should do.
Inviting someone to RECORD a memory is the genuine per-person case and is
untouched. Copy now says photos and videos, which it has always accepted.

A second person opening a group link on a shared device inherited the first
person's name. The backend was innocent: both recent dev share codes have
recipientContributorId None and correctly return a null name. The name came from
localStorage, under a global contributorName key scoped to neither project nor
share code, and the arrival prompt only fired when that value was empty. The
prompt now appears on every arrival on a group link, prefilled from whatever is
remembered, and never on a per-person link. Known limit, accepted: the device id
is also a single global key, so two people truly sharing a device still land on
one contributor row underneath.

"Invite contributor" did nothing, and this predates the week's work.
InviteToRecordModal is z-50 while the timeline lightbox it launches from is a
z-[60] overlay with an opaque backdrop, and the two are siblings in the same
stacking context, so the modal opened and rendered behind it.
AddPhotosToMemoryModal, launched from the same provider, was already z-[70],
which is what made the inconsistency findable. Raised to match.

title: Contributor Google Photos import, working dedupe, and live processing updates
summary: Contributors can import from Google Photos, and duplicate detection actually matches
detail: Share-link visitors were shown a Google Photos tab that could only fail, since every route required an account. Six public routes now cover the full import, and a contributor's Google access is kept only briefly and never as a lasting grant, because they cannot see or withdraw it. The duplicate key had included a file's modified time, which changes when a file is copied, so it matched almost nothing; it is now name plus size, and backfills found 180 duplicate groups already sitting in prod. Contributor video uploads also update live instead of spinning until a reload.
commitMessages:
Contributor Google Photos import, working dedupe, and live processing updates

Three contributor-flow fixes found by testing in prod with real people.

Google Photos was unavailable to contributors. Every /api/google-photos/* route
sits behind verifyToken and a share-link visitor has no account, but the tab was
rendered unconditionally, so contributors were offered something that could only
401. Built the feature rather than hiding the tab: six public share-code routes
covering OAuth, picker session, import and status.

The design decision that mattered is where a contributor's Google credentials
live, and the answer is nowhere durable. The callback keeps only the short-lived
access token, under an opaque handle in a new GPGRANT# row, and discards the
refresh token. Holding a live Google grant for somebody who has no account with
us, cannot see that we hold it, and cannot withdraw it is worth more than the
convenience it buys. The cost is a reconnect per import session and a ceiling of
roughly an hour per import.

Because the surface is public, most of its tests are about what it refuses. The
share code is read from the OAuth state rather than the request body, so consent
cannot be bound to a project of the caller's choosing. A grant handle is scoped
to project AND share code, so one lifted from a link cannot be replayed against
another. The import ignores any projectId in the body. The handle is spent on
use, and import status will not return another project's job.

Worth recording how the investigation went wrong first: the route-entry log line
is written by a global middleware that runs BEFORE verifyToken, so a 401 logs
identically to a success. Reading it as proof the caller was authenticated

Duplicate detection matched nothing. The key hashed in lastModified, which
changes when a file is copied or re-downloaded, so the same photo from a second

key is now name + size, with lastModified stored raw so a stricter key stays

already present in prod.

title: Rebuild YouTube upload as a chunked resumable upload
summary: YouTube upload rebuilt to resume in chunks, ending triple uploads and endless spinners
detail: Uploading a 1GB video produced three stuck copies on YouTube and a dialog that spun forever. The worker loaded the whole file into memory and ran out, the platform retried twice and each retry started a fresh upload, and the crash skipped the code that marks a failure. The file now goes up in 8MB pieces, the upload session is saved before the first byte, and a retry asks YouTube how far it got and continues. A local test killed an upload at 35%, resumed from YouTube's own count, and finished with one video.
commitMessages:
Rebuild YouTube upload as a chunked resumable upload

Uploading a 1089.2 MB video from prod produced three identical stuck videos
in YouTube Studio and a modal that spun forever. Three separate defects.

The worker PUT the whole file in one request with duplex: 'half', which reads
like streaming but applies no backpressure, so S3 delivered faster than
YouTube accepted and memory pinned at exactly the 1024 MB ceiling. No
EventInvokeConfig meant AWS applied its default of 2 retries, each of which
re-initiated the upload and got a fresh session URI, hence three partial
videos from one request. And an OOM kill terminates rather than throws, so
the catch that writes 'failed' never ran; two prod records sat at 'uploading'
forever, one since 2026-05-24.

All three are fixed by one mechanism: ask YouTube where it got to and
continue from there.

- 8 MiB ranged S3 GETs into Content-Range PUTs. Peak memory is now O(chunk).
- The session URI is persisted BEFORE the first byte goes out, so a retry
  resumes rather than starting a second upload. That write ordering is the
  fix for the duplicates.
- Running low on time, the worker re-invokes itself and resumes. Capped at 12
  continuations to stay under AWS recursion detection, whose hop counter is
  per request-chain and not resettable.
- A 200 on the offset query means the upload finished and only our write was
  lost; recovering the id there is what stops that becoming a duplicate.
- maximumRetryAttempts: 1, explicit. Not 0, because a resuming retry is a
  free recovery; not 2, because that was the implicit default being left.

Progress reporting falls out of the chunking: bytes are written after each
chunk, throttled to a 2% step or 3 seconds, and the status route derives the
percent so the panel and the video list cannot disagree.

sweepStuckVideos gains a fourth sweep on a YT#PENDING partition of the
existing sparse GSI. The threshold is 60 minutes but the real guard is an
updatedAt staleness check, since a live upload touches the record constantly.

Two adjacent bugs fixed while in here. "Upload Again" left the old
youtubeVideoId and youtubeUrl, so a poll landing in the gap returned the
previous video's link alongside status 'uploading'. And the 409 guard now
allows a takeover after 5 minutes of silence, which resumes rather than
restarts, so a transient failure no longer locks the user out until the
sweep.

The success panel now says YouTube is still processing and the link will not
play for others yet. YouTube shows an API-uploaded video as "Uploading 0%"
for minutes afterwards, which reads as a failure even to someone who just
watched it succeed in the logs.

Verified end to end locally on a 1 GB video: killed at 35%, resumed from
YouTube's own byte offset (2 MiB ahead of our record, which is the "trust the
Range header" rule earning its place), uploaded the remaining 677 MB, landed
exactly on the total, and produced one video instead of three.

summary: Music starts with the title on card-less videos, edits stop reverting, and dev CI now matches prod
detail: Videos without section cards opened with eight seconds of silence because music started after the first photo; it now begins during the title slide. Trimmed clips appeared to revert because one cache was never refreshed; a single helper now refreshes all of them, and a test fails any hand-written partial refresh. commitMessages:
Start music during the title slide on card-less videos

A short project with no section cards opened with eight seconds of silence
and the music arrived half a second AFTER the first photo.

_open_section_timing gave every section a music_start_ms of
current_ms + SECTION_MUSIC_DELAY_MS. Both builders add the title slide's
duration before any section opens, so for a section WITH a card that 500ms
lands inside the card and music gets the whole card as a runway. For a
card-less video current_ms is already the end of the title, so the same rule
put music after the first photo. Same clock time, opposite effect.

One rule now covers every section: music begins 500ms into the slide that
PRECEDES the section's content. With a card that is the card. For a card-less
FIRST section it is the title slide. Measured on a default project (8s title,
from project.titleSlideDuration), card-less music moves 8.5s -> 0.5s and
carded videos are unchanged. Only the first card-less section borrows the
title, so a later one cannot run backwards over the section before it.

Also deletes beat_sync_mode and music_lead_in_ms from
build_authoritative_timeline. They existed to give a card-less first section
a different start and never once affected the audio:
rebuild_timeline_from_actual_durations has no such parameters, and it is the
REBUILT timeline that music placements are re-anchored to in renderer.py, so
the beat-sync start was computed and thrown away before every mix. The
orchestrator passed music_lead_in_ms=0 outright. A regression test now
asserts both builders agree. The separate beat-sync feature that sets photo
DURATIONS from phrase boundaries is untouched.

Route project item-cache invalidation through one helper

Trimming a clip in the timeline lightbox reported success, but reopening it
showed the original boundaries. DynamoDB held the new ones the whole time.

useOrgDerivedData builds organizationPhotoMap, which is what the lightbox
reads clip boundaries from. It seeds the map from the photos query and then
OVERLAYS the video-builder items on top, and the overlay wins. onClipSaved
invalidated only ['project', id, 'photos'], so that query refetched the
correct values and the untouched video-builder cache stamped the old ones
back over them. useVideoBuilder carries staleTime 60s, so it would not
refetch on its own either. The dev log shows the PATCH followed by
GET /api/photos and no GET /api/projects/.../video-builder.

New utils/queryInvalidation.ts exports invalidateProjectItemData(queryClient,
projectId, {photoId?}), covering photos, photo-library, video-builder,
memories, stats, plus the single-photo detail key. Undefined projectId is a
no-op so route params pass straight in, and it returns the settled promise so
optimistic mutations that await in onSettled keep their ordering. Applied at
24 call sites.

Six more instances of the same bug, found by the audit:
- TimelineV2 excluded lightbox: onSuccess and onClipSaved, photos only
- useUpdatePhoto: no video-builder, so editing a timeline photo's date,
  description, location or section left the timeline showing the old value
- useDeletePhoto: no video-builder and no memories, so a deleted photo
  survived in the timeline cache
- PhotoDetail deletion: photos + stats only
- TimelineV2 section delete: items move back to the library but photo-library,
  the query feeding the Photos tab, was never invalidated
- MobileTimelineView never passed onClipSaved, so a clip trimmed on a phone
  invalidated nothing

Two non-bugs cleared. TanStack v5 matches keys by PREFIX unless exact:true, so
invalidateProjectData in ProjectLayout was invalidating ['project', id] and
then four keys already covered by it; the four are gone. SettingsTab had
['video-builder', projectId], segments in the wrong order matching nothing,
harmless only because the call above it covered everything. Removed, with its
now-unused queryClient.

The helper alone would not have prevented this, since the original bug was a
call site hand-writing a shorter list than its neighbours.
queryInvalidation.test.ts walks the source tree and fails on any raw
invalidateQueries against photos, photo-library, video-builder or memories,
naming file and line. Verified by reverting useDeletePhoto on purpose. stats
is deliberately outside the guarded set: nothing merges it, and
useGenerateVideo is right to invalidate it alone. Two optimistic-reorder
rollbacks in TimelineV2 are allowlisted and now say why they stay narrow.
