Fix clip thumbnails breaking when the trim moves off the frame

Trimming a clip so its thumbnail frame fell outside the new range replaced a
working thumbnail with a broken image. The frame was there the whole time.
The URL was spelled wrong.

media_utils.py names every extracted frame ZERO-PADDED,
f"frame_{second:02d}s.jpg", so GCS holds frame_02s.jpg through frame_16s.jpg.
photoHandler.js rebuilt it unpadded. Trimming a clip to 2-7.8 picks midpoint
4.9, snaps to 4, and wrote frame_4s.jpg against a bucket holding
frame_04s.jpg. It breaks on any single-digit second, so most short clips; the
other nine clips in the test project survived by rounding to 6, 8 and 8. The
reader side was always fine, since /frame_(\d+)s\.jpg$/ parses 06 as 6.

Two more 404s hid on the same line. Frames run from one interval to
frame_count * interval (media_utils numbers them (i+1)*sample_interval and
stops at the video duration), and the old
Math.round(midpoint / interval) * interval was clamped to neither end: a clip
near the start could name frame_0s.jpg, which is never extracted, and one near
the end could name a frame past the last one taken.

The rule now: re-pick the thumbnail ONLY when we can name a frame that was
actually extracted AND that lands inside the trim. Anything less certain keeps
the existing thumbnail, because a frame slightly outside the trim still shows
the clip while a URL for a frame nobody uploaded shows a broken image. New
backend/src/utils/frameNames.js owns the padding, parsing and the
snap-and-clamp; nearestExtractedFrameSecond needs the source video's
frame_sample_interval AND frame_count, and returns null when either is missing.

Four hand-written copies of the padding rule collapse to two, one per language.
media_utils.py exports frame_stem / frame_file_name, used by its own extractor
and by both call sites in gemini_client.py. The backend mirrors it. Both files
name the other. services/video-processor has no test suite, so
frameNames.test.js carries the shared case table and is the only executable
statement of the contract; parity with the Python was verified by running the
same table through frame_stem.

Self-repair instead of a migration: a thumbnail URL that parses but is not in
canonical form is re-derived on the next trim, so bad records fix themselves
as clips get edited. Without it the one currently-broken clip would have
stayed broken, since its frame IS inside its range and the old check would
have called it fine.

Allow a cover photo from outside the timeline

The cover picker only ever offered the photos already in the video. Often the
shot that works as a title slide is one deliberately left out of the timeline.

Not just a picker change. orchestrator.py resolves the title photo from
photo_id_to_local_path and clip_id_to_clip_info, both derived from the VIDEO
ITEMS, so a cover outside the timeline is never downloaded and would fall
silently through to get_last_photo_path. The user would pick a cover, see no
error, and get a different title slide.

Picker: two tabs, "In this video" (the existing grid, still the default,
section accordion intact) and "All photos". Tabs appear only when there are
library photos, so the single-source case looks unchanged. No new query, since
usePhotos already holds every project photo; selectLibraryCoverCandidates
filters an array that is in memory. Wired at both picker sites, the Create
Video modal and the Settings tab.

Dispatch: when titleCoverPhotoId is not among the built videoItems (checked
through memory photos too), videoHandler fetches it and attaches
settings.coverPhoto = {photoId, storagePath, mediaType}. Its own field rather
than a smuggled video item, so it cannot reach the video body or the photo
counts and the renderer never has to ask whether an id is a timeline member.

Renderer: fetch that one object after the main photo download and register it
in photo_id_to_local_path, leaving every branch below unchanged. Deliberately
NOT added to all_photos_to_download, which would run it through face
detection, inflate the progress budget's photo count, and risk it reaching
built_video_items. A failed fetch is never fatal; it logs and auto-selects.

Photos only: a clip cover needs its whole source video downloaded to extract
one frame, so clips stay choosable from the timeline tab where that video is
fetched anyway. A deleted cover still falls back silently rather than failing
a render, and the picker now says the photo is gone.

Two preview paths would have lied. resolveCoverPhoto gains an
explicitOnlyCandidates argument: an explicit cover may be any project photo,
but the FALLBACK must stay "last photo in the last section". Passing library
photos in candidates instead would let one win the fallback, since it carries
no sectionId and would survive to the unsectioned last resort.
MobileTimelineView also scanned only timeline items for its theme preview, so
a cover chosen on desktop previewed the wrong photo on a phone; it now takes
allPhotos, already in useProjectContext, so still no new query.

Already correct and untouched: the sticky-cover rule in eventOrganizerHandler
(its comment already said timeline membership does not matter here), and the
watch page and share OG image, which call getPhotoById directly.

Ships in two halves: the renderer change only reaches production on an EC2
deploy, so release the backend and the renderer together.

summary: Frontend deploys get real cache headers, and the landing animation matches the real sample reel
detail: Frontend files had shipped with no cache headers, so a returning visitor could miss a deploy for hours. Hashed assets are now cached for a year and index.html is always rechecked. The landing hero animation was rebuilt item for item from the published sample reel: 13 real keepers and 4 real rejects. commitMessages:
Give frontend deploys real cache headers

aws s3 sync sets NO Cache-Control unless told to, and neither workflow told
it to. Verified live: index.html and the JS bundle both came back from
CloudFront with no Cache-Control at all. A response without one gets heuristic
freshness from the browser (roughly 10% of its age since Last-Modified, no
revalidation), so a deploy can stay invisible to a returning visitor for hours.
CloudFront invalidation cannot help: it clears CloudFront, not the copy in
someone's browser. DEPLOYMENT.md said the opposite and is corrected.

Two passes now, in deploy-frontend.yml and deploy-prod.yml. Pass 1 takes
everything except index.html with public, max-age=31536000, immutable, safe
because Vite content-hashes those filenames. Pass 2 takes index.html alone with
no-cache, because it is the file that names the current hashes.

--delete belongs on pass 1. Exclude/include filters apply to the DESTINATION
listing too, so a pass filtered down to index.html can prune nothing and stale
bundles would accumulate forever. Pass 1 excludes index.html, so its --delete
leaves the entry point alone and removes only assets no longer built.

Stop the landing sample throwing the page around on play

Clicking play made the page appear to scroll itself, sometimes leaving the
player entirely out of view. Three stacked causes, each hiding the next.

1. THE PANEL COLLAPSED. The stage holding the animation band and the player had
no height of its own; it was whatever its in-flow child happened to be. On play
the band went absolute while the video grew from height: 0, so for a moment
nothing was in flow and the panel fell to its padding, 458px to 70px. That
pulled 388px out of the document and every section below jumped up. Measured,
not inferred: scrollY never changed and no scroll event fired in either the
broken or the fixed case. The page was never scrolling; the document was
shrinking underneath it.

The stage now owns its height and animates between band height and player
height, with both children absolutely positioned so neither can decide how tall
the panel is. Height never passes through zero. The measurement also moved off
the band, the one element whose layout role changes at exactly that moment, onto
the stage, whose width comes from its parent and means the same thing before,
during and after. h-[430px] md:h-[360px] became named constants because the
stage needs them as numbers.

2. SCROLL ANCHORING WAS MOVING THE PAGE FOR US. The invisible one. Chrome
adjusts scrollY to keep visible content still when things resize, which is right
for a late-loading image and wrong for a panel that grows ~200px deliberately.
Measured: scrollY went 668 to 824 with no scroll of ours. overflow-anchor: none
on the scrolling element while playing, restored on cleanup.

3. SCROLLING DURING THE GROWTH DOES NOT WORK. A layout change under an in-flight
scroll cancels it. The scroll now waits for transitionend on the stage's height
(700ms fallback for when the height does not actually change) and measures the
settled panel, so the result is exact rather than predicted from Tailwind
spacing. It centres the panel under the fixed chrome when it fits and top-aligns
under it when it does not, so the top of the video is never behind the nav on a
short window. Verified landing at 124px against an ideal of 123px.

The chrome offset is read from the nearest declared scroll-margin-top rather
than by measuring a bar: #transformation already carries scroll-mt-24 for the
"See How It Works" anchor, so that is the page's own statement of the distance,
and it survives the landing page using <nav> where the app shell uses <header>.

Add a browser smoke suite that runs against a real stage

Beta launch bucket 15. The testing pyramid gets a top: seven critical-path
flows in Playwright, run against local dev, deployed dev or prod, from a
manual workflow that gates nothing.

The recon (reports/2026-09-11-testing-recon/REPORT.md) measured backend 42%

the totals: every route-level page on a critical path sat at 0%, while the

Seven flows, serial, sharing one project that is deleted in afterAll even
when a flow fails partway: sign in, create, upload a photo and a 2s clip,
save a settings change, see the tier gate and dismiss it, create an invite
link and open it in a fresh context, delete. homePage.spec.ts is rewritten

The previous suite was dead, not merely stale: globalSetup clicked a

then ran nothing at all. projectPage.spec.ts was stale in three further ways
and example.spec.ts tested playwright.dev. The three-browser matrix went too;
it tripled every write against real dev data, and the nine orphaned projects
on the old test account were the receipt.

Two constraints the suite lives under. It never accepts a tier-gate prompt,
because accepting logs a probe click, which is the beta's willingness-to-pay

title: Stop deleted projects leaking public thumbnails, sweep the timer bug class, and add a pre-merge CI gate
summary: Deleted projects stopped leaking public thumbnails, and merges now have to pass tests first
detail: Three copies of the delete code had drifted, so deleting a project left its photos, clips, search data and share links behind. One shared version now handles all of it. Cloud Run's video thumbnails sat in a public bucket the backend could not clean, leaving 234 frames from deleted prod projects readable; a narrow permission and a cleanup script brought both stages to zero. A new CI check runs tests before a merge rather than only before a deploy. That exposed a frontend suite failing about half its runs from timers firing after tests ended, which was fixed across 14 components, and 324 skipped tests were deleted.
commitMessages:
One delete cascade, a pre-merge CI gate, and no more skipped tests

Closes parking lot #32, #35 and #36; closes #34 as won't-do; rewrites #33;
opens #39 for the one leak that could not be fixed in code.

#32, the delete cascade. Deleting a project removed its DynamoDB records and
S3 objects and left every photo and clip in GCS. The cause was duplication:
deleteProjectHandler and the admin user-deletion loop each carried a
near-verbatim cascade, and deletePhotoHandler carried a third version of the
per-item half. Only the smallest knew about GCS, so the two that mattered
skipped it. Nobody decided that; it fell out of the copies.

Now one implementation. services/projectDeletion.js holds the cascade and
services/mediaAssets.js the per-item half, with all three callers using them.
The split between those two files is not cosmetic: importing the full cascade
into photoHandler dragged db/videos.js and its db/photos.js import into that
module's graph and broke a test whose mock lacked VIDEO_PENDING_GSI_PK, which
is the trap db/projectCounters.js already documents.

Two more leaks went with it: EMBEDDING# rows, written at upload time for every
item and deleted by nothing, and VIDEO_SHARE# lookup rows, which live under
their own partition key and so outlived their project, leaving a dead
/watch/<code> resolvable. New deleteGcsPrefix sweeps three prefixes across two
GCS buckets, because Cloud Run writes extracted frames to paths no record
stores as a deletable field. The cascade had no tests at all; it now has 16.

#39, opened. Verified against live dev with gcloud rather than trusting logs:
photos/, videos/ and frames/ all went to zero objects for a deleted project,
thumbnails/ kept 4. Cloud Run writes CDN thumbnails under its own identity and
the backend service account has no IAM binding on that bucket, so the fourth
sweep would 403 forever. Omitted deliberately, with a comment and a test
assertion pinning the omission. Needs an IAM grant in both GCP projects.

#36, CI before a merge. Every other workflow runs tests on the way to a
deploy, so they gate the deploy, after the merge, never the merge itself.
ci.yml runs on PRs into main and on pushes to any branch but main, in three
parallel jobs mirroring the pre-push checklist. No cloud credentials, deploys
nothing, and does not run the browser smoke suite.

Adding it exposed a flake that would have made the gate worthless: the
frontend suite was failing about half of all runs with every test passing, on
an unhandled "window is not defined" from React's scheduler after the jsdom
environment was torn down. PhotoUpload.tsx arms three cosmetic setState timers
and cleared none on unmount. Fixed with a ref for the third and one cleanup
for all three; 8 consecutive runs now clean.

#35, 324 skipped tests deleted rather than restored. They asserted against
components since rewritten, and a padded count is worse than a smaller honest
one. The frontend suite is now 1,387 tests with zero skipped.

Stop deleted projects leaking public thumbnails, and sweep the timer bug class

Four loose ends from the delete-cascade work. One was a disclosure, not
housekeeping.

CDN thumbnails (PARKING_LOT #39, closed). Cloud Run writes thumbnails to
thumbnails/<projectId>/<videoId>/ in the CDN bucket under its own identity, and
the delete cascade never swept that prefix because the backend service account
had no binding on either CDN bucket. Both buckets grant allUsers objectViewer,
so a thumbnail outliving its project stays readable on the public internet, and
since that role also carries storage.objects.list you did not need the URL to
find it.

Measured by real set difference against the AdminIndex PROJECT partition, not by
comparing totals: prod 5 orphaned prefixes / 234 objects / 81 MB, dev 36 / 3,520
/ 474 MB. Prod is why comparing totals fails, it has fewer thumbnail prefixes
(46) than live projects (78) and still had orphans.

Closed with a bucket-level custom role, cdnThumbnailReaper (objects list, get,
delete), bound to kindred-reels-gcs@ on both CDN buckets. objectAdmin would have
matched the photos and videos buckets but also grants write, and write on a
public-read bucket means a compromised backend could serve anything from
cdn.kindredreels.com. The fourth sweep is back in projectDeletion.js and its test
assertion is now positive. cleanupOrphanedThumbnails.js cleaned the existing
orphans on both stages, both re-verified at zero; a formerly-public prod frame
now 404s anonymously and a live project's thumbnail still serves 200.

The script is dry-run by default, requires --stage, and always writes a full
per-object manifest before deleting. It aborts on zero live projects or any
prefix that is not a 32-hex project id, which are the two ways this kind of
script empties a bucket.

setState timers. PhotoUpload was one instance of about twenty. Fourteen were
real and are fixed: the "Copied!" flash in every share modal, two self-re-arming
poll loops, the two OAuth popup callbacks that reach for window, the admin
refetch timers, and the timeline drag auto-expand. Four were correctly left
alone and the reasons are in FRONTEND.md. A mounted flag turned out not to be
enough on its own, it stops the setState but leaves the timer pending. Four
regression tests, each verified to fail without its fix.

Node v22.23.0 breaks every authenticated GCS call, and it is not the VPN. It is
a Node patch regression: @google-cloud/storage reaches node-fetch@2 through a
nested google-auth-library@9.15.1 and gaxios@6.7.1, and on that one patch
node-fetch@2 fails on any chunked response with no Content-Length, which is
exactly how Google's token endpoint replies. v18.20.8, v22.5.1, v22.22.0 and
v24.13.0 all pass. No code changed; written up in LOCAL_SETUP.md.

Also opened PARKING_LOT #40: both CDN buckets, and cdn.kindredreels.com itself,
are anonymously listable. Investigated only, no IAM changed. Nothing lists a CDN
bucket at runtime, and the narrowing needs no custom role since
roles/storage.legacyObjectReader is exactly storage.objects.get.

title: Stop queued jobs outliving their project, and close two more public CDN leaks
summary: Queued jobs no longer retry forever after their project is deleted, and a second public leak closed
detail: Checking the thumbnail fix on prod found two video-analysis tasks retrying for over a day against a deleted project, at attempts 42 and 43 of 100, paying for 85 analyses that could never succeed. The worker now checks the source still exists and reports the job as obsolete, and the queues now allow 3 attempts instead of 100. The frames sweep had always looked in the wrong bucket, so every deleted project's frames stayed public; the code was fixed and 636 prod objects removed. The backend role also gained the permissions it needed to list and delete stored files.
commitMessages:
Stop queued jobs outliving their project, and close two more public leaks

Verifying yesterday's thumbnail fix on prod turned up a retry storm. Pulling
that thread found three more defects.

Two Cloud Tasks had been retrying for a day against a project deleted the day
before, at attempts 42 and 43 of a possible 100. Each attempt re-downloaded the
source, re-uploaded thumbnails and frames to a world-readable bucket, and paid
for a Gemini clip analysis before dying. 85 paid analyses for two videos that
were never going to succeed. The trigger is an OOM: the container exceeds its
8Gi limit and Cloud Run kills it, so the task is never a 2xx and never stops.

Three separate things were wrong.

The worker did work nobody wanted. process_video now checks the source object
still exists before anything expensive and returns 200 with
{"skipped": "source_missing"} when it does not. A missing source means the
project or video was deleted, so the job is obsolete, and reporting obsolescence
as an error is exactly what makes Cloud Tasks retry. Guarding in the worker
rather than cancelling tasks on delete is deliberate: it also catches a task
already dispatched, which cancellation cannot, and it needs no deterministic
task names whose one-hour tombstone would break re-uploading the same video.

The queue outranked the application. sweepStuckVideos gives a pending video
three attempts then marks it failed; the queues allowed 100. Both are now 3 with
a 60s backoff floor instead of 0.1s, which bounds any deterministic failure
rather than just this one. The queues are not IaC-managed, so the settings and
the command to re-apply them are in INFRASTRUCTURE.md.

The OOM itself is untouched and is now PARKING_LOT #41.

The frames sweep had never worked. Cloud Run writes storyboard frames to
gs://<CDN bucket>/frames/<projectId>/<videoId>/, next to the thumbnails, and the
delete cascade swept frames/ from the VIDEOS bucket where that prefix has never
existed. Same disclosure class as the thumbnails and larger: prod had 47 frame
prefixes publicly readable. VIDEO_RENDERING.md had it right all along; the code
and its test shared the same wrong idea, which is why the test passed.

The Lambda role could not list S3, so both S3 prefix sweeps failed on every
delete. s3:ListBucket is a bucket-level action needing the bare bucket ARN and
the role had only object-level grants; the videos bucket also had no
DeleteObject at all. Fixed in serverless.yml, so it reaches a stage only on that
stage's next backend deploy.

The prod smoke suite could never have passed. blockAnalytics aborted the Google
Analytics requests, and an aborted request logs net::ERR_FAILED, which F1's
zero-console-errors assertion caught. Dev never hit it because deploy-frontend
builds dev with an empty VITE_GA_MEASUREMENT_ID, so nothing requests gtag there.
The helper now fulfils those routes with an empty 200: nothing reaches Google
either way and the assertion stays strict instead of growing an allowlist.

Cleanup, both stages, dry run and manifest first. cleanupOrphanedThumbnails.js
is now cleanupOrphanedCdnMedia.js and reaps both roots, because a script
covering one of two identical leaks is a trap. Removed dev 37 prefixes / 11,925
objects / 125 MB and prod 6 prefixes / 636 objects / 20 MB, on top of the
thumbnails cleared earlier. Both re-verified at zero, thumbnail and frame prefix
counts now match exactly, and a formerly-public prod frame returns 404
anonymously.

Also verified: the CDN thumbnail sweep works in the deployed Lambda. The dev
smoke run's own project logged
"GCS prefix sweep gs://kindred-reels-cdn-dev/thumbnails/<id>/: 2/2 deleted".

title: Close the parking lot's last three items: CDN listing, the 8Gi OOM, and orphaned project rows
summary: Closed the last three parking-lot items: public bucket listing, an 8K memory crash, and orphaned data
detail: The public file buckets could be listed by anyone; they now allow only fetching a known file, checked step by step on dev and prod. The suspected memory leak was really an 8K video, so clips are now capped at 4K with limited threads, using 64% less memory and running 3.9 times faster. Orphaned project data turned out to be wider than search rows: 7,715 leftover rows on dev and 785 on prod were removed. The cleanup refused to run when it found test debris in the dev table, and that check was kept strict.
commitMessages:
Close the parking lot's last three items

All three were parked as correct-but-bigger-than-the-change-in-hand. Two turned
out smaller than feared and one was a different bug than its title said.

#40, the CDN buckets were anonymously listable. allUsers held
roles/storage.objectViewer, which carries storage.objects.list as well as get, so
both buckets enumerated without credentials, including through
cdn.kindredreels.com because the load balancer passes the S3-compatible XML list
API straight to the bucket. Swapped to roles/storage.legacyObjectReader, a stock
role holding exactly storage.objects.get. No custom role needed. Dev then prod,
verified at each step: JSON list 401, XML list via the load balancer 403, direct
object GET 200, cache-busted GET through the load balancer 200, landing sample
200, backend authenticated listing unaffected. The cache-busted request is the
one that matters, since a cached object would have served either way.

#41 was not a memory leak, it was an 8K video. The clip that OOM'd the 8Gi
container is 7680x4320 HEVC, 33 megapixels a frame, 2.9 seconds long. It died in
the transcode, where ffmpeg ran with default thread counts and each thread holds
full-resolution frame buffers. The renderer's largest output is 4K, so an 8K
intermediate was pure waste. Capping at 3840x2160 and pinning decode AND encode
to 2 threads took peak RSS from 3.51 GiB to 1.27 GiB and the run from 8.87s to
2.29s, measured on a reproduction of the failing input.

Bounding the decoder is what did most of it and is easy to miss: -threads after
-i only reaches the encoder. Two threads cost nothing in wall time even at the
worst supported input, a 120s 4K source. Two edge cases checked rather than
assumed: a 640x480 input stays 640x480, because the filter uses min() against
the source and never upscales, and 1081x721 comes out 1080x720 because libx264
needs even dimensions.

#42 was wider than its title. Filed as orphaned EMBEDDING# rows, but the bug is
that a project PARTITION outlived its project and every row type in it is
equally stranded. Reaping only the noticed type would have left the rest and
stopped anyone looking. cleanupOrphanedProjectRows.js deletes the whole orphaned
partition and reports the breakdown: dev 176 partitions / 7,715 rows across 14
types, prod 7 / 785 across 5. Both re-verified at zero; dev went from 229
PROJECT# partitions to 49, matching its 49 live projects.

The scan the write-up worried about was a non-issue: 22k-27k items, a few
seconds, projecting PK and SK only so the 1408-dim vectors never cross the wire.
The orphan test needs two independent signals, no METADATA row AND absent from
the AdminIndex, because either alone can be wrong.

Two guard rails earned their keep. The dev run refused to start on four
partitions whose ids are not project ids, including PROJECT#undefined and the
frontend test fixture id: nine-month-old debris in the real dev table. Deleted
by explicit key rather than by loosening the guard, which was right to stop. And
the first prod delete threw ProvisionedThroughputExceededException after 733
rows, because every row in a partition shares one PK and a large partition is a
hot key while being deleted. The script handled UnprocessedItems but not a
thrown throttle; it now handles both, paces batches, and being idempotent the
re-run finished the remaining 52.

commitMessages:
Stop setting state on modals after closing them

The pre-push hook caught an unhandled error from DraftMemoryModal. All 1,392
tests passed; the error came from a promise resolving after the test environment
had shut down.

The code saved a recording, closed the modal, then set state on the modal it had
just closed:

    onSuccess();
    onClose();               // unmounts
    } finally {
      setIsUploading(false); // runs afterwards
    }

Nine instances across five files, found by looking for a finally that sets state
inside a handler whose try calls onClose, onSuccess or navigate: both memory
modals, AddPhotosToMemoryModal, NewProject and ContributeBrowse.

Where the handler always closes, the reset moved into catch, which is the only
path where the component is still on screen. That is what the code meant all
along: if we are leaving, there is no flag left to reset. Three cases need a
local flag instead: removing the last photo dissolves the memory and closes
(twice), and ContributeBrowse navigates from inside the try with a return, which
does not skip the finally.

RotateControls matches the shape and is NOT a bug. Its onSuccess refreshes the
photo but leaves the control on screen, so resetting its flag is correct.

This is the same class as the setState-timer sweep the day before, reached a
different way, and that sweep could not have found it: it counted setTimeout
against clearTimeout, and here there is no timer, just an async continuation
resuming after unmount. Both shapes are now written up in docs/FRONTEND.md.

What is not proven: with the bug deliberately restored it would not reproduce,
0 in 35 runs, so it needs full-suite parallelism and the right timing. Ten clean
runs afterwards are consistent with a fix but do not demonstrate one. What is
certain is that the line named in the crash no longer runs on the path that
closes the modal.

Also here:

CLAUDE.md gains two rules. "You Wrote All Of This Code" says never to frame a
defect as pre-existing or not mine; there is one developer on this project and
when a bug appeared matters only as a clue for fixing or prioritising it.
"Write Plainly" asks for ordinary words and for explaining a thing rather than
naming it.

The beta launch tracker is caught up: bucket 15 (testing pyramid) closed now the
smoke suite is green against prod, buckets 4, 5 and 9 given done items and
archive pointers, a pre-existing bucket 12 status mismatch corrected, and the
target launch window moved to end of September 2026.

sectionCardsEnabled, turns them off, shown in two places that share the one

The renderer was built for this. video/timeline.py derives section boundaries
from each item's section_id, never from the presence of a card, and it already
had a music-start rule for a card-less first section. So the renderer change is
one thing: build_section_ordered_items takes section_cards_enabled and skips

every section's duration with the card's duration, and the picker places music

runtime estimate drops the same term for the same reason.

The default is on, which makes || wrong at every read site: stored || true can

the toggle would look broken while the stored value was right. Every site uses

Say when a cover photo has no preview

Joe reported the cover thumbnail in Create Video looking broken. The plan blamed
the two consumers preferring opposite fields: the picker reads
`thumbnailUrl || url`, the preview reads `url || thumbnailUrl`, so one could work
while the other failed. Scanning both stages killed that theory. Across 5,893 dev
photos and 11,562 prod photos there is not one case where the two disagree about
whether the image loads.

It was a video clip. A clip has no storagePath and no thumbnailStoragePath, so
cdn_thumbnail_url is its only image, and 110 of dev's 466 timeline clips point at
cdn.kindredreels.com. That host fronts the PROD bucket and nothing else, so a dev
record holding it asks prod for an object that only exists in dev and 404s
forever. Prod has 13. Reproduced in Chrome on dev's Disney World 2018: 29 broken
images on the timeline page, 10 of 22 selectable cover tiles blank.

The padding bug fixed in September is the minority of this, 34 of 156 dead dev
URLs. The rest are spelled correctly and still dead, which is exactly why the
repair never fired on them: it looks for a misspelled frame name or a frame
outside the new trim, and a canonical URL inside range passes both.
isCurrentFrameUrl is the test that catches them, so a clip now heals the next
time anyone edits it. The repair is skipped when GCS_CDN_BUCKET is unset, because
buildFrameUrl would otherwise write the string "undefined" into the host path and
replace one dead URL with another.

The defect worth fixing is that nothing checked whether the cover loaded. Three
surfaces drew it, none had an onError, and one draws it inside a sandboxed iframe
where a 404 is completely silent. So a dead URL rendered the browser's
broken-image glyph surrounded by a UI insisting everything was fine, and the one
error state that existed checked whether the photo id resolved, not whether its
image was alive.

The copy was corrected before shipping. The first draft said the cover could not
be shown and the video would pick one instead. That is false: the renderer
resolves the cover from the photo's S3 object, or by extracting its own frame

problem and the copy says so. A test asserts on that distinction.

Record where the strangers came from and why their videos failed

Two recons, both findings only, no code.

The first traces 30 strangers who signed up on their own from 2026-08-22

Stop losing videos to a NaN, a negative fade, and a deleted record

Three defects found by reading prod, all live until now.

Music duration. Library MUSIC# records store `duration` in seconds; user
USER#/MUSIC# records store `durationMs` in milliseconds and carry no
`duration` at all. videoHandler read `musicTrack.duration * 1000` for both, so
a user-uploaded track produced NaN, the DynamoDB marshaller refused it, and
the whole createVideo write threw. The user got a 500, no VIDEO# record, and
no way to tell what went wrong. Every stranger who has ever uploaded their own
music hit this: three of them, 28 failed attempts, one pressing the button 14
times in an hour before filing "I press to make a video and it doesn t work".
Both read transforms now emit both units so no call site has to know which
table a track came from, and an unreadable duration is a 400 rather than a
write that cannot land.

Credits fade. render_credits_slide passes a fixed 1.5s fade-out, and Settings
lets someone pick a 1-second credits slide, which is the smallest value the UI
offers. That built fade=t=out:st=-0.50, FFmpeg rejected the negative start, and
the render died. clamp_slide_fades now bounds both fades inside the segment, in
models.py rather than at the call site, so no caller can produce a negative
start whatever it passes. The UI minimum stays 1 second; the renderer is
responsible for its own safety.

Nothing watched any of it. Bucket 2's failure monitoring only covers failures
after a VIDEO# record exists, and both of the above fail before one does. A
5xx on generate now emails the founder with the project, owner and size,
throttled to one per project per hour so fourteen presses do not send fourteen
emails. Expected 4xx paths stay silent.

videoGenerated no longer reads only live VIDEO# records, so deleting a
finished video stops erasing the evidence it existed. Three stranger projects
rendered, downloaded and deleted, and the funnel counted all three as never
having generated anything. first_video_completed_at is written once by the
renderer, which owns the only status:complete transition, and is best-effort
so a lost analytics attribute can never fail a video already in S3.

Plan moving the render payload to S3, with the ceiling measured

Defect 2 from the same recon: a project large enough to push its video job
over DynamoDB's 400KB item limit cannot render at all. Researched and designed
only, nothing built.

The ceiling is measured rather than guessed. Across 83 prod VIDEO_CONTENT#
records the cost is 1,134 bytes per photo or clip at the median and 1,476 at
the worst, so the record fails between 277 and 361 items. KK's Bat Mitzvah
dispatched 323 and failed eight times. The scaling variable is photos and
clips, not top-level videoItems entries, because a memory can wrap many
photos; using the wrong denominator makes the cost look wildly variable when
it is not.

S3 over gzip, and the reason is the clip exclusion. gzip compresses these
payloads 5.2 to 7.6x, which clears 1,000 items. But MAX_UPLOADS_PER_PROJECT
deliberately does not count derived clips, and limits.js puts those at about
20% of items, so a project legitimately at the cap holds roughly 1,200 rows.
gzip lands at 76 to 83% of the budget there, with no room for one new
per-item field and none to raise the cap. It moves the ceiling; S3 removes it.

The delete cascade is the real risk and it has three paths, not one. Research
also turned up a pre-existing leak: deleteVideoHandler removes both DynamoDB
rows and never deletes the rendered mp4, though s3Key is in scope. Fixing that
is in scope for the implementation.

One IAM change, on the Lambda only: the videos bucket grants GetObject and
DeleteObject but not PutObject. The renderer needs nothing, because its role
carries AmazonS3FullAccess, which is itself worth a look in bucket 4 along
with an inline policy that names dev buckets while running on prod.

All five open questions answered by Dimitri and recorded as decisions. Bucket
5 picks up the one deferred item: what the maximum supported project size
actually is, since the renderer becomes the binding constraint once DynamoDB
stops being one.

Move the render payload out of DynamoDB and into S3

A stranger with 327 photos pressed "Make video" eight times. Every attempt
died on the PutItem in createVideo with ValidationException: Item size has
exceeded the maximum allowed size. No VIDEO# record was written, so nothing
in the product or the funnel recorded that anything had happened.

Measured on prod across 83 records before changing anything: the cost scales
with photos plus clips, not with top-level videoItems entries, at a median
1,134 bytes each. That puts the failure point between 277 and 361 items,
while a project can hold about 1,200 rows. gzip was measured as the cheaper
fix and rejected: at 76-83% of the limit it clears today and leaves room for
nothing.

The payload now lives at render-payloads/<projectId>/<videoId>.json in the
existing videos bucket, about 1.4MB at the cap against a 5TB object limit.
Write order is the object, then the VIDEO_CONTENT# sibling holding the
pointer, then the VIDEO# record, so everything is written before anything
that points at it. One write path, no size threshold; both older inline
shapes are still read, so there is no migration.

The sibling records payloadS3Bucket next to payloadS3Key, because the
renderer's S3_VIDEOS_BUCKET default is the dev bucket and a prod instance
missing that variable would otherwise read the wrong bucket.

Also fixed here, found while tracing the delete paths: the single-video
delete never removed the rendered mp4. deleteVideoHandler had video.s3Key in
scope and unused, so every video deleted on its own left its file in S3
until the whole project was deleted. The delete moved into deleteVideo
itself so no caller can forget it.

One IAM change: s3:PutObject on the videos bucket for the backend Lambda.
The renderer needs nothing, its role already has AmazonS3FullAccess.

Deploy the EC2 renderer BEFORE the backend. A backend writing pointers to a
renderer that cannot follow them fails every render.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01SdctwPzyCoQ3Akc1c2PQ5H

Delete projects in a worker, and let the renderer see faces

Two defects from the 450-item dev run.

Deleting a large project timed out and left it half gone. The cascade ran
inside the request and at 450 photos it is about 1,350 external calls: an S3
delete, a GCS delete and an embedding delete per photo. That is past the 30s
Lambda timeout, and raising the ceiling was not available either, since API
Gateway's HTTP API caps the integration at 30s without a quota increase. The
product allows 1,000 uploads per project, so this was reachable in ordinary
use.

DELETE now marks the project and answers 202, and the cascade runs unchanged
in a new projectDeletionWorker Lambda with one retry. Retrying is safe because
every step is a delete, per-step failures are already swallowed, and the
PROJECT# record goes last, so a retry finds less to do.

The mark REMOVEs the UserProjectsIndex keys rather than setting a flag the
list could filter on: that index is sparse, so the project leaves the owner's
list at once and costs nothing at read time, and its INCLUDE projection cannot
carry status because DynamoDB will not extend an existing GSI projection.
adminPk and adminSk stay, so a project stranded by a dead worker is invisible
to its owner but still findable by an operator. The mark is awaited before the
invoke so a failed invoke still leaves the user seeing the project gone.
Project routes 404 a deleting project, checked once in checkProjectOwnership.

Separately, the renderer could never call Rekognition. The instance role had
no Rekognition permission in its inline policy or any of its eight managed
policies, so DetectFaces returned AccessDenied on every render on both stages,
logged at WARNING while the render continued. Face data drives the Ken Burns
focus point and crop bounds. The grant is applied by hand, since that role is
not in IaC. The same path also wrote face_data where the backend writes and
reads faceData, so a success would have been discarded and re-billed on the
next render; both halves are fixed.

Not covered and logged in the tracker: the admin delete-user route loops the
same cascade over every project a user owns and has the same problem, worse.
It needs orchestration rather than a fire-and-forget invoke.

Record that a release deploys the renderer second

deploy-processing declares needs: deploy-backend, so tagging a release deploys
the backend first and the renderer after it. That is sequencing rather than a
data dependency, and it is the safe order most of the time: do not ship a
renderer if the backend failed.

title: Deploy the renderer before the backend on a release
summary: Releases now deploy the renderer before the backend
detail: The renderer reads what the backend writes, so it has to be updated first, but the release workflow did the opposite and any render started in the gap failed. Twice the prod renderer had to be deployed by hand ahead of a release. The workflow now deploys the renderer first, with a guard so a manual run that skips the renderer still deploys the backend. Releases are slower, and dev merges still race, which was recorded as a known gap.
commitMessages:
Deploy the renderer before the backend on a release

The renderer READS what the backend WRITES, so the reader has to be upgraded
first. deploy-prod.yml had it backwards: deploy-processing declared
needs: deploy-backend, so a tag shipped the backend and the renderer caught up
several minutes later, and every render started in that gap fails.

Two changes have had that shape already, the 2026-08-03 SQS pointer and the
2026-09-14 S3 render payload. Both needed the prod renderer deployed by hand
ahead of the tag. An instruction written in two docs that the pipeline actively
works against is not a safeguard.

deploy-processing now hangs off validate and deploy-backend waits for it.
Shipping a newer renderer alone is always safe, since it handles every older
payload shape, so nothing is given up by putting it first.

deploy-backend's `if` is load-bearing and should not be simplified to a plain
needs:. deploy-processing is SKIPPED on a manual dispatch unless
skip_processing is explicitly false, and GitHub skips the dependents of a
skipped job, so the condition treats skipped as a pass. Without that, a manual
dispatch with default inputs would deploy nothing and still report success.

Two deliberate consequences: a release is slower, because backend and frontend
now wait on the slowest job, and a failed renderer deploy blocks the backend
rather than landing after it.

Does not fix dev, where deploy-backend.yml and deploy-processing.yml are
separate path-filtered workflows that still race on a merge. Noted in
DEPLOYMENT.md.

commitMessages:
Show the cover photo on a phone

Reported from a phone: a project appeared to have no cover photo and no way to
set one. It had one. titleCoverPhotoId was set, the photo was in the timeline
with valid storage paths, and the video used it. The phone just could not show
it.

GenerateVideoModal gates its whole Cover Photo block on `timelinePhotos` being
non-empty. TimelineV2 passes it; MobileTimelineView passed only coverPhotoUrl.
So on a phone the section never rendered: no preview, no Change button, and no
empty state saying why. The four other props the picker needs were missing too.
Mobile now passes all five.

A second bug surfaced while fixing it. Mobile had its own hand-rolled copy of
the cover resolution instead of using utils/coverPhoto, and the copy disagreed
with the renderer: with no cover set it previewed the FIRST photo in the
timeline, while the renderer falls back to the LAST photo in the LAST section.
The preview therefore showed a photo the finished video would not use. The copy
is deleted in favour of resolveCoverPhoto, which carries that fallback itself.

Neither is a regression from the S3 payload release; these files were untouched
by it. This is the mobile view drifting from the desktop one, the same shape as
the tracked gap where mobile cannot remove a timeline item.

Guarded at the prop boundary, which is where the defect was. Four of the five
new assertions fail against the old code, including the fallback one.

NOT verified visually: Chrome would not give me a viewport under the 767px
breakpoint, so the mobile branch never rendered locally.

summary: The Create button in Choose Video Length stays on screen on phones, and dev deploys now run renderer first, like prod
detail: On a phone the Create button in the length picker sat under the bottom navigation and could not be scrolled into view. Three layout faults caused it: the overlay ran under the nav, the panel height ignored the nav, and the scroll box grew instead of scrolling. All three now match the other dialogs, and the button is pinned to the bottom of the scroll area, checked by measuring in Chrome at a 375px width. commitMessages:
Keep the Create button on screen in the timeline length step

On a phone the button in "Choose Video Length" was cut off by the bottom nav
and could not be scrolled into view. Three things were wrong and all three
had to go.

The overlay was `fixed inset-0`, so it was laid out against the whole viewport
and its lower edge sat under the nav. The panel capped at max-h-[90vh], and vh
is the full viewport: it knows nothing about the nav bar, nor about the
collapsing URL bar on iOS Safari. The scroll box had no flex-1 min-h-0, so it
sized to its content and grew past the panel rather than scrolling inside it;
min-h-0 is the easy one to miss, because a flex item defaults to
min-height:auto and refuses to shrink below its content.

All three now match GenerateVideoModal and ThemeBrowser. Measured in Chrome at
375px: the overlay ends at 611 where the nav starts at 610, and the panel caps
at 595 rather than 600.

The button is pinned as well, so it is reachable without scrolling past every
option. sticky rather than a real flex footer because it renders in three
branches of the component and hoisting it would push that branching up into
the modal for no visual gain.

One thing measuring caught that reasoning would not. A sticky offset resolves
against the scroll container's PADDING box, so inside a p-6 container bottom-0
pinned the bar 24px above the visible edge with content scrolling through the
gap underneath: probe bottom 579 against a scroller bottom of 603. -bottom-6
sits it flush, verified at 603 = 603 and holding position across the whole
scroll range.

Also corrects a claim in the previous entry: Chrome does produce a sub-767px
viewport. Screenshots come back at devicePixelRatio 2, and 1530x784 was
misread as CSS pixels rather than 765.

Order the dev deploys the way prod orders them

Prod was fixed earlier today to deploy the renderer before the backend. Dev
still raced: deploy-backend.yml and deploy-processing.yml each carried their
own push trigger, so a merge fired them as two independent runs with nothing
sequencing them.

In practice that was worse than a coin flip. The backend reliably wins because
it is the faster job: 2m09s against 3m29s on one merge, 2m05s against 3m03s on
the one before. So the wrong order was the normal outcome, and a merge carrying
a change only a newer renderer understands broke dev renders for the length of
the renderer deploy.

A new deploy-dev.yml owns the trigger and calls the two in order. They are
CALLED rather than merged into one file, because their job bodies are long and
copying them would risk a silent transcription error in the place hardest to
test. Both keep workflow_dispatch so either surface can still be deployed
alone.

Two things that are easy to get wrong. The changes job works out which surfaces
actually changed, because the trigger's path filter only decides whether the
workflow runs; without it a backend-only merge would also redeploy the
renderer, starting a stopped m6i.4xlarge and paying its idle timeout for
nothing. And deploy-backend must treat a SKIPPED deploy-processing as a pass,
since GitHub skips the dependents of a skipped job: as a plain needs:, a
backend-only merge would deploy nothing and still report success. Same trap as
the prod guard.

The changes job fails safe both ways: with no usable base commit to diff
against it deploys both surfaces, because deploying neither would look like a
green run that shipped nothing.

CLAUDE.md claimed a merge fires four independent workflows. Corrected there.

title: Run one deploy at a time, per target
summary: Every deploy workflow now runs one at a time per target, after two runs nearly broke the dev renderer
detail: Merging the previous PR fired two push events for the same commit 31 seconds apart, and both runs began copying renderer code onto the same EC2 machine at once. The duplicate was cancelled and the machine survived only because the right run finished its copy last, by seventeen seconds. Every deploy workflow now has its own concurrency group, so a second run waits instead of overlapping. Unlike CI checks, deploys are never cancelled midway, since that would leave half-copied files on a live machine. The called workflows got separate group names so a manual renderer redeploy is also covered without deadlocking the caller.
commitMessages:
Run one deploy at a time, per target

Merging the previous change produced TWO push events for the same commit, 31
seconds apart. Both Deploy Dev runs started and both began deploying the
renderer to the same EC2 box at once. That job wipes ~/video-processor/src,
copies over SSH, then restarts systemd, so two interleaving can leave half the
code on the box with the service running on it.

The duplicate was cancelled by hand and the box came out intact, but only
because the surviving run finished its copy LAST, by seventeen seconds. That is
luck, not a safeguard.

Every deploy workflow now carries a concurrency group, so a second run queues
instead of running alongside the first. cancel-in-progress is false on all of
them, the opposite of ci.yml: cancelling a CI run discards an answer to a stale
question, while cancelling a deploy kills it midway through writing files to a
live box, which is the state being guarded against.

The two workflows deploy-dev.yml calls carry groups of their OWN. The caller's
group serialises runs of itself but cannot see a run of the renderer workflow
started straight from the Actions tab, which is a normal thing to do and lands
on the same box. Distinct from the caller's rather than shared, because a
reusable workflow sharing a concurrency group with its caller deadlocks: the
caller holds the group while waiting for the child that needs it.

deploy-cloud-run.yml and e2e-smoke.yml are left without one. Cloud Run deploys
are atomic revision swaps where the last simply wins, and the smoke suite is
manual dispatch only.

The exposure was not new. The separate per-surface workflows that existed
before had the same hole; nothing had happened to hit it.

title: Let the delete worker start, and notice when a worker cannot
summary: The new project delete worker actually runs, and a worker that dies before starting now emails the founder
detail: The background worker that deletes projects shipped and never completed a single delete: it crashed on load because a face-service import pulled in an image library the worker did not have. The library now loads only inside the one function that uses it, and a new test walks every Lambda's imports and fails if one without that library can reach it. A new failure handler runs outside the failing worker and emails the founder when a background job dies before its own error handling can run. The fix also found that the delete never removed per-user preference rows, now part of the cascade. Only two internal test projects had been stuck, and prod ended with 83 projects and zero orphaned rows. The PR also added the customer-emails skill describing how the founder writes to users.
commitMessages:
Let the delete worker start, and notice when a worker cannot

projectDeletionWorker shipped in v0.1.23 and never completed a single delete on
any stage. It died in INIT with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for sharp.

The worker imports services/projectDeletion.js, which imports
services/rekognitionService.js for deleteProjectCollection, which had a
top-level `import sharp from 'sharp'`. sharp is excluded from the bundle and
supplied by sharp-node-layer, and the worker has no layers. ESM evaluates a
top-level import eagerly, so pulling in one Rekognition delete call dragged in
an image library and killed the function before it ran a line. The cascade
never touches sharp.

sharp now loads lazily inside cropToFace, the only function in that file that
uses it. It is already async and its only caller already awaits, so no
signature and no caller changed. The worker needs no layer at all.

Two reasons this reached prod, both now covered:

- projectDeletion.test.js mocks rekognitionService.js wholesale, so the import
  that breaks was never loaded. New lambdaNativeDeps.test.js walks the static
  import graph of every function in serverless.yml and fails if one without the
  layer can reach sharp. Verified by reverting the fix: it fails and names the
  chain. Dynamic import() is not counted, so the fix does not read as the bug.

- An async invoke that fails twice disappears with nobody listening. New
  asyncWorkerFailure Lambda is wired as the onFailure destination on
  projectDeletionWorker and youtubeUploadWorker. It runs outside the failing
  process, which is what makes it work for a worker that could not start, and
  emails through the existing sendFailureNotification path.

Re-driving the two stranded prod projects surfaced a second gap: the cascade
never deleted USER_PREFS# rows, leaving one per user behind every delete. Same
shape as the EMBEDDING# gap in PARKING_LOT #42. deleteUserPrefsByProjectId is
now a cascade step and deletes all rows under the prefix, since a project with
contributors holds one per person.

Blast radius was 2 projects, both internal test projects, found by scanning all
26,494 prod rows for status = deleting. Zero on dev. Nothing was lost. Prod is
now 83 live projects, 83 partitions, 0 orphans.

Also adds the customer-emails skill, which captures how founder-to-user email
gets written: short, no recount of the investigation, lead with who you are,
say it is still in beta, link deliberately, draft never send.

title: Crop vertical clips by measuring the file, not the record
summary: Vertical phone clips are cropped to fill the frame instead of appearing as a thin strip
detail: In finished videos, many vertical clips showed as a 9:16 strip using 32% of the width. Phone video is usually stored landscape with a flag that says to rotate it, and the app recorded the raw landscape size, so the renderer thought the clip was not vertical and skipped the crop. The renderer now measures the downloaded file itself and swaps width and height when it is rotated a quarter turn, which fixes every existing clip on its next render with no backfill. The same wrong size meant the clip analysis never asked where the action was in rotated video, so only 18 of 400 sampled clips had a crop centre. On the real prod video the strip went from 32% of the width to a 56% square, which is deliberate so cropping does not throw away what people want to see.
commitMessages:
Crop vertical clips by measuring the file, not the record

Vertical clips were landing in the landscape frame as a thin strip. Nothing was
reverted: `git log -S "clip_height > clip_width"` shows the gate untouched since
5cfb30d. It had never worked for the most common kind of vertical video.

Phone video is nearly always a landscape 1920x1080 stream carrying a rotation=-90
flag. probe_video recorded that raw stream size, so a portrait clip was written
down as 1920x1080, the renderer asked `clip_height > clip_width`, got no, and
skipped the crop. FFmpeg then auto-applied the rotation on decode anyway, so the
frame turned portrait and got letterboxed.

Measured in prod, project 51de06ea ("Ramnagar trip"): 5 of 13 source videos carry
rotation=-90, and cropdetect on the delivered video finds segments of exactly
404x720 inside a 1280x720 frame. 32% of the width.

Two fixes, because one root cause broke two things.

The renderer now measures the file. New probe_display_dimensions and
build_clip_crop_filter in processing/src/video/segments.py; the payload's
videoWidth/videoHeight are only a fallback for when the probe cannot answer. This
is self-healing: every clip already in the database crops correctly on its next
render, with no backfill.

probe_video is rotation-aware in services/video-processor/src/media_utils.py, so
is_vertical in gemini_client.py is right and actionCenterY is actually computed
for new uploads. It never was for rotated video: only 18 of a 400-clip prod sample
had a value. The face-aware centring was not being bypassed, it was never being
calculated.

Verified on the real prod file through the real filter chain: content box 404x720
-> 720x720, 32% -> 56% of the frame width. Square rather than wider is deliberate:
cropping harder starts throwing away video people want to see.

_ClipSlideReader (clips inside memories) already decided from frame.shape[:2], the
decoded frame, so it was never affected. That asymmetry, one path trusting the file
and the other the database, was the actual design flaw. Both now trust the file.
Do NOT add a transpose filter: FFmpeg applies the display matrix before user
filters, so the frame reaching crop= is already upright.

17 new tests covering every rotation form, probe failures, and the gate itself.
Verified against the pre-fix logic: 5 fail, including the one named for the bug.

title: Write down who we emailed, so the next wave does not repeat itself
summary: An outreach log records every email sent to users, so the next wave never contacts someone twice
detail: Twenty-one emails went to real beta users on Sep 15 in two waves, all sent by hand, and the only record of who got what was one ignored local file. A new outreach record, the mirror of user feedback, stores each email sent, with an admin page and a last-contacted column on the users list. It keeps the Gmail thread id so replies could be read later, and a channel field so sending from the app can be decided later without changing records. Sending and automatic reply detection were left out on purpose, because the feedback inbox had shown that more screens do not get things read. A Gmail labelling rule was written down, and the backfill of all 21 emails ran on both stages.
commitMessages:
Write down who we emailed, so the next wave does not repeat itself

Twenty-one emails went to real users on Sep 15, in two waves: six replies about
render failures and feedback, then fifteen asking beta users how their video came
out. All of it was composed and sent by hand in Gmail. The only record of who got
what was one gitignored report file, and that file is the sole reason the evening
wave knew to skip the six people contacted that morning. It would not have
survived a third wave.

New OUTREACH# entity, shaped after FEEDBACK#, which is its mirror: feedback is
mail they sent us, outreach is mail we sent them. Sixth consumer of the AdminIndex
via adminPk='OUTREACH', and no index change was needed, because adminPk is a type
discriminator designed for exactly this.

Three things about the shape are deliberate:

- adminSk mirrors sentAt, not createdAt, unlike every other AdminIndex consumer.
  The entity is backfilled from mail sent before it existed, so ordering by
  row-creation time would put the whole backfill at the top of the list and bury
  anything recent. There is a test pinning this.
- gmailThreadId is stored on every row even though nothing reads it yet. Today it
  is a click-through to the thread. Later it is the hook that lets a job read reply
  state out of Gmail without a reconstruction pass. Cheap to capture at send time,
  expensive to recover afterwards.
- channel ('gmail' today, 'ses' reserved) exists so the open question of whether
  sending moves into the app can be answered later without changing any record.

Deliberately not built: sending, automatic reply detection, and a replies-waiting
badge. Replies land in the inbox as ordinary mail, so that signal already reaches a
human. What genuinely had no home was who-was-contacted and what-was-learned. The
lesson driving that scoping is the feedback intake: it was built, it worked, and
three submissions still sat unread for 16 days. More UI was never the missing piece.

Adds an AdminOutreach page copied from AdminFeedback, a "last contacted" column on
AdminUsers derived in memory rather than stored on USER#, and backfillOutreach.js
to seed the rows from a ledger that stays gitignored because it holds real email
addresses. Backfill has been run on both stages, 21 rows each.

The Gmail side is a labelling convention, written down in OPERATIONS.md 4.1: every
outreach thread carries both `Outreach` and `Outreach/<Campaign> <Month> <Year>`.
The parent has to be applied explicitly, because Gmail's label:Outreach does not
match sublabels, and that search is what stands between the next wave and emailing
somebody twice.

usersHandler.test.js needed fixing rather than writing: it mocks every db module
the handler touches, and the new outreach import was not among them. Note that
jest.clearAllMocks() wipes implementations in that file, which is why it
re-establishes each mock's resolved value in beforeEach.

title: Serve pages a crawler can actually read
summary: Public pages are prerendered so search engines and AI crawlers can read them for the first time
detail: Strangers had been finding the site since late August, yet every public URL served the same empty shell with 37 characters of visible text, and robots.txt, sitemap.xml and llms.txt all returned that shell too. Public routes are now prerendered at build time with a headless browser, the landing page went from 37 to about 5,200 characters of visible text, and the three crawler files exist as real files. Pages use trailing-slash addresses to avoid a redirect, and each prerendered page carries a small guard so deep links into the app do not flash the landing page. Two workflow fixes came with it: a one-year cache rule would have frozen the new pages, and CI had to install a browser to build. A check script now fails if a page stops being readable.
commitMessages:
Serve pages a crawler can actually read

Every public URL returned the same 2,523-byte shell with 37 characters of
visible text, identical for Googlebot and GPTBot. Five public pages were
byte-identical to the homepage, so they looked like one page at six URLs, and
robots.txt, sitemap.xml and llms.txt each answered 200 with that shell, which
looks like success and is not.

The three missing files needed no CloudFront change. The SPA fallback only
fires when S3 returns an error, so a file that exists is served straight
through; they returned the shell because they were not in the bucket.

The public routes are now prerendered at build time. scripts/prerender.mjs
drives Playwright (already a devDependency) over vite preview and writes
dist/<route>/index.html. The landing page went from 37 characters to about
5,200, and each page carries its own title, description and canonical.

Three things here are load-bearing:

- URLs gained trailing slashes. Output lands at dist/about/index.html, and the
  S3 website endpoint answers /about with a 302 to /about/. Measured on dev
  with a throwaway probe, after confirming dev and prod sit on identical
  origins. Canonical, sitemap, llms.txt and every internal link use the slash
  form so nothing a crawler follows takes that redirect.
- dist/index.html is also the SPA fallback, so prerendering it would have made
  a deep link to /projects flash the landing page until React routed away.
  Each prerendered file carries a small inline guard that empties #root when
  the path does not match the page it was rendered for.
- Capture happens before any write. vite preview serves dist/, so writing the
  root file mid-run changed what the fallback returned for routes not yet
  captured, and every sub-page inherited the root's guard.

The deploy workflows needed two fixes. Their cache rule gave everything except
the root index.html a one-year immutable cache, which would have frozen the
prerendered pages and the three crawler files in visitors' browsers. And
npm ci installs the Playwright package but not the browser binary, so every
workflow that runs npm run build now installs chromium first.

/how-it-works/ is prerendered but held out of the sitemap while it is still a
placeholder: crawlable if found, not advertised, deliberately not noindex.

scripts/checkCrawlability.mjs asserts a distinct title, description and
canonical per route plus a 400-character floor, so "five pages that look like
one" cannot come back quietly. Verified against the dev deploy.

title: Show the reel in a shared link, not a logo
summary: A shared video link previews an image from the reel instead of the site logo, and uses the user's own story
detail: Sampling four live share pages, three showed the generic site card instead of anything from the video. Covers were often unset, clip covers resolved to nothing, and using the original photo would have been too large for link previews, which cap images near 5MB. The preview image is now chosen once when the share is created, in the same order the app uses for covers, and stored on the share so each crawler visit costs one read. A backfill stamped the links already sent to families: 23 of 24 on prod. The description now falls back to the story the user wrote, since none of 21 shared projects had a subtitle. The PR also added tagged signup links and made the social preview image generated from a template rather than baked pixels.
commitMessages:
Show the reel in a shared link, not a logo

Sampling four live prod share pages, three showed the generic site card instead
of anything from the video. That is the moment a user is proudest of the
product, and the recipient was getting a logo and a tagline.

Three separate causes, found in order:

- No cover chosen. The image came only from project.titleCoverPhotoId, and two
  of the four had that and projectCoverPhotoId both null, with nothing on
  VIDEO# or VIDEO_SHARE# holding an image.
- A cover that is a clip resolved to nothing. The only test was storage_path,
  and a clip has none; its cdn_thumbnail_url pointed at a perfectly good public
  image that was discarded.
- The obvious fix would have been worse. Stamping the original file looked
  right until the sizes came back: 1.7MB to 21.4MB, against ~445KB for the
  large thumbnail of the same photo. Unfurlers cap og:image near 5MB, so a big
  original renders nothing at all.

Resolution now prefers the large thumbnail, then the CDN thumbnail (a clip's
only image), then the small thumbnail, and uses the original only when no
rendition exists. It happens ONCE, at share creation, stamped onto VIDEO_SHARE#
as previewImageUrl. Not per request: the watch page is public and hit by every
crawler and link unfurler, resolving reads the project's whole photo partition,
and ProjectionExpression does not reduce RCU. That is the read shape that cost
$43 in June.

The fallback order matches frontend/src/utils/coverPhoto.ts, which calls itself
the single source of truth for covers: last photo in the last section, then
last clip, never the first item, because the title slide plays first.

backfillSharePreviewImages.js covers shares already sent out, which is the
point: those are the links real people have already given their families. Dry
run by default, idempotent, never overwrites. Dev: 15 stamped, 9 left alone,
0 failed; a second run stamped nothing.

Also in here:

og:description on share pages used videoSubtitle, and ZERO of 21 shared prod
projects have one, while all 21 have a story. So every shared video showed the
site-wide blurb while the sentence the user wrote went unused. Now falls back
to the story, whitespace collapsed and truncated at 200 on a word boundary,
since a minority use that field as a brief rather than a caption.

signupRef tagged links: six agreed tags in KNOWN_REFS and OPERATIONS.md 2.3.2.
The capture-and-record chain was already built and works (one dev user carries
watch-end from July); what was missing was anything producing a tagged link.

title: Measure whether anyone watched the reel
summary: The funnel now measures whether anyone played, finished, downloaded or rewatched a reel
detail: The funnel stopped at sharing, a high bar for personal videos that almost nobody cleared, so nothing showed whether people liked what they got. Counters on the video record and the share record now track plays, watch-through milestones, downloads and repeat views, written as simple atomic adds rather than a new event log. Watched means 90% of the reel itself, not counting the credits. Repeat views on public links need no viewer id: the browser remembers on its own whether it has played before. Three numbers worked at once from existing data, such as 5 of 19 finished dev reels put on YouTube, and a per-video drill-down explains odd figures. Testing found two bugs before merge, including one that would have stuck the repeat marker forever.
commitMessages:
Measure whether anyone watched the reel

The funnel stopped at "video shared", which is a weak proxy for whether
anyone liked what we made them: sharing is a high bar for sentimental
content and almost nobody clears it. Nothing recorded whether a reel was
played, watched through, downloaded, or watched again.

Counters on records the funnel snapshot already reads, not a new event
log. Owner plays and downloads land on VIDEO#, public watch-page plays on
VIDEO_SHARE#, both via atomic ADD built like recordShareView. Per-event
rows would have needed an AdminIndex partition the snapshot reads in
full, which is fine for a few hundred probe clicks and wrong for playback.

Four decisions worth keeping:

- "Watched" means the reel, not the credits. Milestones measure against
  content duration (total minus the credits slide) and completion fires
  at 90% of it, the way Netflix counts an episode.
- Repeat viewing needs no identifier. The ownership gate already proves
  who the owner is; on the public page the browser answers about itself
  from localStorage and sends a boolean. No viewer id is ever created.
- A play session is one opening of the player. The owner's player
  autoplays, so play_count is named and read as "times they opened it".
- Downloads are counted on both surfaces, on separate records. The owner
  keeping their own reel and a recipient keeping someone else's are
  different facts and are never summed.

Reporting splits the same way. YouTube uploads (since Feb), share-view
depth (since Jul) and return-to-create (since the first project) had full
history and read correctly on day one; the watch-through curve starts at
zero and the page says so. Both the overall and stranger cuts are stored,
because snapshots are immutable and writing one loses the other forever.
Return-to-create is computed over every project owner rather than the
AdminIndex user partition, which is forward-only from Jul 20 and would
have silently discarded most of the answer.

A per-video drill-down behind GET /api/admin/engagement answers which reel
produced a number that looks wrong. It is the only live read on that page,
loaded from a button, and stays out of the snapshot so trend history keeps
its size guard.

Two bugs found by testing rather than reading: a corrupted localStorage
value wedged the repeat marker permanently, and the share update sent an
ExpressionAttributeValues key its expression never referenced, which
DynamoDB rejects outright. Both have tests.

Nothing here can be backfilled. Playback counters start at zero on deploy.

commitMessages:
Project last_played_at, so the per-video table stops reporting null

`last_played_at` was written to the video record correctly from the start, but
never added to the ProjectionExpression in loadProjectVideoStats. I added
`first_downloaded_at` there and missed its sibling. DynamoDB returns only
projected attributes, so the per-video drill-down saw undefined and reported
null for every video.

Nothing rendered the field, so no number anyone read was wrong and no stored
data is affected. The reason it is worth more than a one-line commit is the
failure mode: a missing projection entry throws nothing and logs nothing, and
looks exactly like the feature not working. It surfaced only because someone
watched a reel on dev and noticed a null beside counters that had clearly moved.

So the fix is one identifier, and the guard is the point. funnelStats.test.js
pins the projection against the lists its readers actually use, deriving counter
names from config/engagementEvents.js rather than hardcoding them, so a counter
added there and not projected fails a test instead of aggregating as zero
forever. Confirmed the new test fails with the fix reverted.

Also records PARKING_LOT #51, found while verifying: a video whose S3 object is
gone fails silently in the player, no error and no message. Dev expires video
objects after 30 days, so 101 of 106 completed records there point at nothing.
Prod has no such rule and no user has lost a reel this way.

detail: Recompute on the admin funnel page had returned an error on both stages since July, because the API role was never allowed to call the snapshot function. commitMessages:
Let the admin Recompute button actually invoke the snapshot Lambda

Pressing Recompute on /admin/funnel returned a 500 on prod. The api Lambda
role's lambda:InvokeFunction permission is an explicit per-function ARN
allowlist, and funnelSnapshot was never on it:

  AccessDeniedException: ...-prod-api is not authorized to perform:
  lambda:InvokeFunction on resource: ...-prod-funnelSnapshot because no
  identity-based policy allows the action

I added POST /api/admin/funnel/recompute in July 2026 and did not add its
target to the list ten lines away in the same file. It has been broken on
both deployed stages since.

Two reasons it went unnoticed for two months, both now written into the
comment beside the list:

- The nightly schedule was never affected. EventBridge invokes that Lambda
  directly and does not use this role, so daily snapshots kept arriving on
  time and the page always had data. Only the manual button failed.
- Local dev cannot reproduce it. recomputeFunnelHandler runs the job
  in-process when it is not in Lambda, which is the path every local test
  takes.

Same class of bug as the per-index DynamoDB ARNs, which INFRASTRUCTURE.md
already warns about in nearly identical words: scoped resource lists fail
only at runtime, and only once deployed. That warning now exists for the
invoke list too.

Also fixes the error banner on that page, which is how this stayed
mysterious. It used raw Tailwind dark-palette classes (bg-red-900/30,
text-red-300) instead of the theme tokens the rest of the app uses, so in
the light theme it rendered pale pink on pale pink. The message was there
the whole time and could not be read. Now text-danger on bg-danger/10 with
role="alert", checked in the browser rather than asserted in a test.

Corrects a claim I made yesterday: the dev videos 30-day expiry is NOT
undocumented. INFRASTRUCTURE.md has covered it since 2026-08-04, symptom
included. PARKING_LOT #51 now points there and narrows to the part that is
genuinely uncovered, that the player shows nothing when a file is missing.

Stop a leaky test leaving an upload in flight past teardown

MemoryModal's "should show uploading state while saving recording" resolved
its mock on setTimeout(100) and then returned immediately without awaiting
it. The upload therefore completed AFTER the test file's jsdom was torn
down, and the chain of failures from there is why this was confusing:

  1. the success path calls setShowRecorder(false)
  2. that setState needs `window`, which is gone -> ReferenceError
  3. the handler's own try/catch catches its own ReferenceError
  4. the catch calls setIsRecordingUploading(false), which throws again
  5. that one escapes as an unhandled rejection

So the reported stack pointed at the CATCH block, which made it look like an
error-path bug. It is not. The error path was never involved; the trace was
just the second throw.

Fixed where the leak is. The mock now hands back a deferred, the test resolves
it explicitly inside act(), and nothing is in flight when the test returns.
Also removes a real 100ms wait.

Measured before and after, because this is timing-dependent and a single
green run proves nothing: roughly 1 full-suite run in 3 produced the
unhandled error before (reproduced on main too, so it predates the current
work), and 10 of 10 are clean after.

It was blocking the pre-push hook intermittently.
