title: Timeline quality: six sessions on how a video gets built
summary: Six sessions of timeline-quality work: better picks, correct dates, clips judged like photos, easier editing
detail: About 30 strangers found the site from late August, and hand-reviewing the 23 timelines they made showed the pipeline choosing the wrong items and too many of them. One curator now runs for every video length, photo scores carry a decimal so they stop tying, weak photos are dropped by a rule in code, and video clips get the same judgements and gates as photos. Sideways video is now detected at import by asking only whether a picture is upright, which also cut per-photo upload cost from $0.00359 to $0.00134. Dates got fixed at the root: the capture time inside every video had never been read, and six sort orders became one. The cover photo is chosen as an opening shot, one call picks how the video opens and ends, and removing items and seeing why something was left out got easier. A check for photos and clips of the same moment was built and switched off, and the length picker now says 'up to' instead of promising a count.
commitMessages:
One curator for every tier; retire the separate quick curator

Quick mode ran its own combined architect+curator because it has no
architect and no naming pass, so something had to author a title,
subtitle and mood. The two prompts then drifted, and quick lost three
things standard had:

  - No clip target at all. Quick passed targetClips: null, which
    disables BOTH guards in resolveCuratorResult, so a project with a
    budget of 6 clips shipped 78.
  - No theme fan-out. The whole pool went in one call, so nothing
    spread the picks across moments.
  - No singleton misfit filter, skipped on the grounds that "quick's
    curator has the not_relevant guardrail" -- which both curators
    build from the same buildExclusionGuardrailBlock, so the reason
    never distinguished them.

Quick was 15 of the 23 timelines the stranger cohort produced, so the
drifted path is the one nearly every new user gets.

Quick is now "one section, quick's budget" and otherwise identical.
Title and subtitle come from sectionNamingService off a curator-authored
summary, gated by curatorAuthorsNaming (deterministic OR quick), which
also sets includeSummaryMood. quickCuratorStep.js is deleted; nothing
imported it and no test covered it. The user's per-section description
moves into the shared prompt as buildUserGuidanceBlock, wording
unchanged.

This also removes a live bug on a path nobody in the cohort hit: a quick
project with a user-chosen section count skipped skipArchitect but still
routed to the quick curator, so each section self-named in isolation and
the naming pass then overwrote all of them from empty summaries.

Verified on dev, Disney World 2018 - 2 and Outer Banks 2024, both tiers.
Clips landed exactly on target in all four runs (Disney quick kept 14 of
116 candidates against a target of 14); totals within budget; titles,
moods, music and covers all present; no exclusion missing a reason or a
stage.

Bucket 17 "Timeline Quality" added to the beta tracker as a launch gate,
superseding the 2026-08-07 decision not to track curation quality -- its
own revisit condition was "if evidence demands", and the cohort
evaluation is that evidence.

Cap images per Gemini call in the curator and the singleton filter

PIPELINES.md has said "never send 150+ images in one call" since June,
with the measurement behind it (0/3 blocked at 150, 3/3 at 300). Only
the thematic stage ever enforced it. The curator had no cap at all.

Measured on the Sept 2026 stranger cohort: quick mode sent up to 483
images in a single curator call, and even after moving quick onto the
theme fan-out the largest single theme was still 287.

Curator: CURATOR_MAX_ITEMS_PER_CALL = 100, matching the thematic stage's
margin. runCuratorStep becomes a wrapper over runCuratorCall. At or
under the cap it makes exactly one call and behaves as before; over it,
the pool splits into contiguous chronological chunks that share the
pool's budget via the same computeThemeBudgets used for themes, run in
parallel, and merge. Three properties keep a chunked call
indistinguishable downstream, each with a test: chunks are contiguous
and merged in order so chronology survives; budgets sum to the target so
chunking cannot inflate a section; and the chunks yield ONE cover
nominee, since a chunk is not a theme and must not add a row to
coverNominees. Chunked calls take the tight allowed range
(buildResponseFormatBlock gains tightRange, defaulting to !!themeContext
so nothing changes today) -- the +2 overshoot is per call, so a loose
range across K chunks would sum to +2K on one budget.

Singleton filter: SINGLETON_FILTER_MAX_CANDIDATES_PER_CALL = 40, lower
for a second reason on top of image count. That stage makes the model
account for every candidate id exactly once, and the bookkeeping
degrades with N. Verifying phase 1 yesterday, 87 candidates in one call
came back with 86 accounted for, so the section failed open and got no
misfit pass at all. Batches now run in parallel against the same
reference winners, and a failed batch costs only its own candidates.

Verified on dev. The 87-candidate call is now 3 calls of 29 and finds 12
misfits where it previously found none. Curator chunking was exercised
end to end by temporarily lowering its cap to 30 and re-running Disney
quick: a 164-item theme split into 6 calls whose budgets summed exactly
to the target (7 photos, 9 clips) and merged to 8 and 9; every curator
call came in under the cap. Cap restored before commit. Outer Banks on
standard is unchanged, every section's clips on target.

Give the curator merit to one decimal place

computeMeritScore rounded the composite to an integer, which flattened
the curator's ranking onto an 11-point scale that most photos crowd the
top of. Across the 3,698 scored photos in the September stranger cohort,
46% scored exactly 8 and 76% scored 7 or above, so on nearly half the
corpus the curator was choosing between items it had been told were
identical.

Measured on Outer Banks 2024 (dev), 120 scored photos:

  distinct values   10  ->  28
  biggest tie       54 photos (45%) at 9  ->  41 (34%) at 8.5

That 54-photo tie splits into 8.5 (41), 9.0 (7), 8.8 (5), 9.3 (1). Three
quarters of what the curator read as a "9" was really an 8.5.

The decimal is lossless for the usual four dimensions: every mean of four
integers is a multiple of 0.25, so 8.0 / 8.3 / 8.5 / 8.8 stay distinct.
Sub-scores stay whole, as the model reports them. The label forces one
decimal (Merit: 9.0/10) so every label is the same width and two scores
compare digit for digit.

Also made the prompt's merit bands continuous. "7-10 / 4-6 / 0-3" put a
6.5 in no band once the composite gained a decimal; they now read "7.0
and above / 4.0 up to 7.0 / below 4.0", with a test that keeps them
gap-free. The keep-zero sentence around MERIT_KEEP_ZERO_BAR still reads
correctly ("no photo here reaches 4/10") and is unchanged.

The frontend debug panel computes this mean independently rather than
calling computeMeritScore, so it was updated in step; a comment now says
so, since it would silently diverge if MERIT_WEIGHTS ever stopped being
equal.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Crz4FhSbHCtoUPVi2b6zaV

Enforce the merit keep-zero bar per item, in code

MERIT_KEEP_ZERO_BAR has existed since June but only as prompt text, and
the sentence it sits in is group-level: "if no photo HERE reaches the
bar, keep none". A 3.0 photo in a group whose best is a 9.0 was never
addressed by it, and the same paragraph explicitly invites the model to
override the score. Three sub-4 photos reached real timelines in the
September stranger cohort, two of them in opening sequences.

New meritFloorStage.js, pure code, per section, after the singleton
filter and before the curator. Two rules keep it from doing harm:

  - A thin section keeps its weak photos. Removal stops the moment the
    remaining pool (photos + clips) would fall below the section's own
    total target, because coming up short is worse than one weak photo.
  - An item with NO merit is never a candidate. That covers photos
    analysed before the feature shipped and, until session B, every
    clip. Absent evidence is not evidence of weakness.

Removals go weakest first, ties broken by id so two runs over one pool
agree. A missing target removes nothing rather than guessing, since
guessing would mean guessing in the direction that throws photos away.

New reason low_merit and stage merit_floor. No existing reason fit:
low_quality is documented as technical faults only, and merit is
explicitly aesthetic, so reusing it would tell a user their photo is
broken when it is not. For the same reason the badge ("Weaker shot") is
styled like "Not Selected" rather than like a defect. The detail is the
upload analysis's own meritReason sentence.

The group-level prompt sentence stays exactly as it is. It is a
different and still useful judgement, and it is what makes an all-weak
group return nothing.

Verified on dev. Outer Banks quick dropped 5 photos (2.8, 2.8, 3.3, 3.5,
3.8) from a 105-item pool against a target of 30, each carrying its own
reason; one of those, the 3.8, rounded to 4 before phase 2 and would
have cleared the bar. Disney is the control: 238-item pool, target 30,
so ample headroom, and zero removals because none of its photos carry
merit data at all.

Let near-duplicate survivor choice see merit

Neither half of the choice consulted highlightMerit. The model's pick
came from a label carrying only a description and a visual signature,
and the deterministic fallback tiebroke inside a quality bucket on the
lexicographic photo id -- in practice a string sort on a random hex
identifier, since almost every candidate is `good`. That is how a 9.00
lost to an 8.75 and a 7.50 lost to a 6.50 in the September cohort: the
pipeline was picking the survivor of a near-duplicate group at random.

Prompt: each photo label now carries the same Merit line the curator
sees, plus one sentence telling the model to prefer the higher merit
between otherwise-similar photos. The pick is still never overridden in
code. To keep the two image-aware passes from drifting in wording or
precision, the line comes from a new shared buildMeritLabel in
curatorPrompts.js rather than a second copy.

Fallback: pickRepresentative sorts quality bucket, then merit
descending, then id. A photo with no merit ranks -1, so it sorts below a
genuine 0.0 without being conflated with one.

Measured on dev: 9 of 20 multi-photo clusters on Outer Banks 2024 now
resolve to a different representative, every change moving to the higher
merit (8.5 -> 9.0, 8.0 -> 8.5, 8.3 -> 8.5, 8.0 -> 9.0). Two of those
four were impossible before phase 2, since 8.0/8.5 and 8.0/8.3 both read
as "8" under the integer score. Disney World 2018 - 2, whose photos
predate the merit feature, changes 0 of 45 clusters, so the id fallback
still governs unscored pools.

Note on the 45%: pickRepresentative only runs when the model picked
nothing or the call failed, so that figure is how often the deterministic
fallback would now choose differently, not how often a shipped timeline
changes. The prompt change is the larger lever and is not measurable
without a controlled comparison.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Crz4FhSbHCtoUPVi2b6zaV

Guard section budgets: clamp to pool, never ship empty, record the tier

Three changes to how a section's budget is decided and recorded.

1. Clamp the target to the pool. computeBoundedProportionalTargets
divides a budget across sections and never compares a target to the
section's own pool; worse, its spread clamp pulls a SMALL section's
target UP toward its neighbours, so a 2-item section can be asked for
11. 19 of 51 cohort sections were asked for at least as many items as
they held. Each section's total is now capped at the items that actually
reach its curator, before the photo/clip split. The shortfall is
deliberately NOT redistributed -- keep it simple, revisit if videos come
out noticeably short -- it is logged, and the clamped numbers are what
SECTION# stores, so the diagnostic matches what the curator was asked.

2. No empty section while the pool holds usable items. New
sectionTopUp.js: after the theme fan-out aggregates, a section under
min(MIN_PER_SECTION, clamped target) is refilled from its own pool,
highest merit first (unscored last), skipping anything whose similarTo
points at an item already in the section, then re-sorted
chronologically. Topped-up items lose their exclusion record.

This overrides resolveCuratorResult's respect for an intentional empty
selection at the SECTION level only. Per-theme calls may still return
nothing -- that is the merit floor working, and the guard there is
unchanged. It cannot hold for a whole section because the renderer skips
an empty section, so the chapter simply vanishes: 6 of 51 cohort
sections came back with zero or under a third of target from a pool of
5+, two of them chapters the user had titled themselves. The pool it
draws from is post quality-gate, content-value, singleton-filter and
merit-floor, so nothing those stages rejected can come back.

The watch-item comment this closes is in curatorResult.js, not
constants.js as the spec had it.

3. Persist the tier. config.videoLength lived only on the organize
draft, which apply deletes, so no project recorded which length mode
produced its timeline and the September evaluation had to infer it from
section counts. Apply now writes lastTimelineVideoLength onto PROJECT#,
named to match lastTimelineStageCounts and written in the same step.
Forward-only, no backfill: null means a pre-2026-09-18 timeline or none.

Verified on dev with 8 forced sections on Outer Banks at comprehensive,
which is exactly the small-section shape these guards exist for. Five of
eight were clamped (worst: target 17 against a pool of 6), one was
topped up (kept 4, filled to 5), and the result had zero sections whose
stored target exceeds its pool and zero empty sections. A section that
kept only 1 photo but 7 clips was correctly left alone: the floor counts
items, not photos. Applying that draft confirmed
lastTimelineVideoLength went from null to "comprehensive", and replaced
the Outer Banks dev timeline in the process.

Document how to detect a user removal, and finish correcting the report

Removing an item from the timeline clears PHOTO#.sectionId
(memoryHandler.js:1098-1099). Any analysis that reconstructs "what the
pipeline picked" as "items that have a sectionId" therefore subtracts
every user removal before it starts, and reads removals as zero. That is

Detect and correct sideways video at import, by asking only whether it is upright

A video filmed sideways whose file declares no rotation was invisible end to end.
ffmpeg applies the rotation a file DECLARES, so the metadata case has always worked;
the case with no metadata reached clip analysis sideways, read as landscape so no
actionCenterY was requested, and rendered sideways. One user's finished video has 78
of 102 items playing sideways.

orientation.py checks before any frame is extracted, and on a correction forces a
transcode with the rotation in the pixels. Thumbnails, storyboard frames and clip
analysis then read the transcode. The renderer needed no change: it follows the clip
record's gcsUri, which apply points at the transcode, and re-probes the file anyway.

THE QUESTION CHANGED, AND THAT IS THE SUBSTANCE OF THIS COMMIT

It started as a copy of the photo path's head-direction observable, which validated at
94% in June on photos OF PEOPLE. Measuring it anywhere else killed it:

- Its premise fails silently. Asked which way heads point in a picture with no heads in
  it, the model names a direction rather than declining. Of 78 photos rotated in dev, 23
  had no face detected, and the ones with no human at all were wrong every time. I opened
  them: a horse walks on a beach upside down, a dog lies on its side.
- Left versus right is a coin flip even with a clear subject. Seven frames of a genuinely
  sideways video split 4 "left" to 3 "right", two corrections 180 degrees apart.
- Four manufactured rotations of one video all returned "270". RotBench (arXiv 2508.13968)
  explains it: models "consistently default to labeling ambiguous rotations as
  counter-clockwise". It puts Gemini-2.5-Pro at 0.50 for 90 degrees and 0.40 for 270 and
  concludes MLLMs cannot identify image rotation.

What every model IS reliable at is recognising upright, 1.00 at 0 degrees in RotBench. So
the question is now "is this image upright?", asked of the frame and of its three
rotations, taking the one that comes back upright. That is RotBench's normalized rotation
voting, which took GPT-4o from 0.19 to 0.86 at 270. Eight test videos covering upright,
90, 180 and 270, with and without people: 8/8, against 4/8 for the head-direction design
on the same files. The corrected outputs were opened and checked by eye.

It short-circuits on the un-rotated frames, the ~98.5% case, so a video costs three cheap
calls and twelve at worst. And it runs on the LITE model: on 16 real photos in all four
orientations, 3.1-flash-lite and 3.5-flash score identically, 16/16 upright and 15/16
rotated. The stronger tier existed for left-versus-right; the new question retires it.

A rotation is applied only when every sampled frame calls it upright and no other rotation
does. Two rotations both reading upright means near rotation-invariant footage — a close-up
of the moon was the real case — and nothing is corrected. Any failed call stands the whole
thing down.

TWO DEFECTS FOUND ON THE WAY

- The shared Gemini client was not thread-safe. Check-then-assign: three threads each built
  a client, the last assignment won, and collecting the losers closed their transports
  mid-request. It broke two of the first three calls. Now locked.
- The transcode would have overwritten every corrected video's date. Re-probing the output
  picks up ffmpeg's own container timestamp, and the callback uses creationTime to overwrite
  exifDate, so every corrected video would have sorted to the end of the timeline. The
  source's value is carried across, pinned by a test.

Forward-only: nothing backfills existing videos. The photo path still uses the old question
and is the next commit; its orientation call has never been cost-tracked and is the larger
half of what analysing a photo costs.

Verified: ruff clean, 66 python tests, 1,964 backend tests, backend lint and import check
clean. The 8/8 run and the eyeball checks were against dev media, no prod data.

Judge clips the way photos are judged, on the call already being made

A photo has arrived with three judgements the pipeline acts on since June:
qualityGate, contentRole and highlightMerit. A clip arrived with none of them, so
filterByQualityGate, filterByContentValue and the merit floor all skipped clips in
silence. Across the 23-timeline stranger cohort, 31% of all timeline items were clips
that nothing had ever judged.

The clip-analysis prompt now asks for the same three, with A.1's exact field names,
nested as geminiAnalysis on the candidate. The nesting is the point: it is the shape the
organizer reads a PHOTO's analysis from, so the photo code gets reused on a clip rather
than copied and the two cannot drift apart in how they judge. No extra model call.

CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED

The added prompt text does not change clip yield. Sixteen dev videos, same session,
prompt with the judgements against prompt without: 11 clips either way. Individual
videos differ by one in both directions, which is variance at temperature 0.2.

Validation fails open PER FIELD: invalid or missing is omitted, never defaulted, and the
clip is never rejected over these fields. A defaulted qualityGate is a verdict nobody
reached; a defaulted contentRoleConfidence would start deleting clips, since the
content-value gate drops on the pair. That path fired for real in the run below: one
clip's merit failed to parse, it kept its other three judgements, and it survived.

MEASURED OVER ALL 164 READY DEV VIDEOS: 140 clips, 140 carrying judgements

  Disney       78 clips  72 good / 6 marginal / 0 reject   65 people 13 place
                         merit 3.5-9.5 median 7.5, 1 under the 4.0 bar
  Outer Banks  62 clips  62 good / 0 reject                52 people 8 place 2 detail
                         merit 3.0-9.5 median 8.2, 3 under the 4.0 bar

Zero rejects and zero functional, and that is the expected shape rather than a broken
prompt. Clip analysis has ALREADY picked the single most memorable 5-10 seconds of each
video before anything is judged; every photo is judged as uploaded. So the two gates will
remove almost nothing from clips in phase 3, and the merit floor is the one that will
bite. All six marginal clips are dark or shaky ride footage; all four under the merit bar

be, since engagement is 0 with no person in frame. Confidence came back high on all 140,
so the gate's confidence distinction is inert for clips. Noted, not tuned.

Free text is capped at 160 characters, not for tidiness: every clip candidate rides on
the organization draft, one DynamoDB item against a 400 KB cap, and the largest dev
project carries 116 of them on a draft already at 250 KB. That is 31 KB of headroom
rather than 54 KB.

The apply step ENUMERATES fields rather than spreading the candidate, so createPhoto
needed a gemini_analysis parameter for the blob to reach the record at all. A clip has no
upload of its own, so apply is the only write it ever gets. Pinned by a test, because a

during the analysis phase rather than uploaded, so they had never passed through

equivalent photo was removed before curation started.

because phase 2 gave clips the photo path's exact field names, and there is now an
explicit test asserting both shapes read the same field, so a rename on either side
fails there rather than in production.

A gated clip is NOT dropped from the candidate array. It stays carrying its reason, so
the excluded-clip accounting still finds it and it appears in Not Included with the
right badge. The tier recommendation and the estimated length are counted after the
gates, so a clip that will never be curated cannot inflate either.

so the weakest items in a section go first whatever kind they are. Ranking them

  content-value gate    0 excluded
  merit floor           4 excluded (1 Disney, 3 Outer Banks)

already picked the best seconds of each video before anything is judged, whereas every

shots, which is what the merit definition implies, since engagement is 0 with nobody in

already called `not_relevant`, listing the same examples. Which word a user saw depended
on which stage caught the item first. Worse, `functional` was not in the badge's reason

so "Not Selected" (75px), "Redundant" (63px) and September's new "Weaker shot" (72px)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H

Show the same file once, however many times it was uploaded

Five of the 23 projects in the September cohort shipped byte-identical images
under different ids inside one finished video, and one did it 35 times. Nothing
in the timeline pipeline had ever asked whether two items are the same file, so
every stage treated the copies as two separate photos.

New fileContentHash answers "same bytes?" where deviceFileKey answers "same
name, same byte count?". The second is needed because the first structurally
cannot cross the Google Photos line: all 5,353 prod imports store originalName
as a synthetic google-photos-<id> and throw the real filename away. Items are
grouped by union over both keys, so a record written before hashing and one
written after still meet through name and size. An item with neither is never
grouped with anything.

Videos get their identity for free and photos do not, which is not a choice. A
photo's stored object is rewritten in place during processing, HEIC to JPEG and
sideways to upright, so its checksum afterwards describes the processed image;
the hash is taken in the worker while the original is still in memory, and only
for new uploads. A video's source.mp4 is never overwritten, so the checksum GCS
computed on upload is still readable today, for videos uploaded months ago.

Which copy stays is decided by the user's own work, not by quality, since the
bytes are identical: the manual cover, then a memory, then a caption, then a
corrected date, then the earliest upload, then the id. The surviving id is the
one the cover choice and the memory point at.

Nothing is deleted and no upload is blocked. The copies that are not kept go to
Not Included with a pointer to the one that stayed. The tile reads "Same file"
and the lightbox "Same file, uploaded twice": the tile caps its label at about
twelve characters, and its tooltip carries the detail line anyway. A duplicate
video has no tile of its own, so its clips carry the reason, annotated after the
clip gates so the duplicate reason wins over a quality one.

Verified on Mom & Pop Turn 70 (10 repeated files, 12 extra copies, the earliest
kept every time) and end to end on Outer Banks 2024 with a controlled copy.

- A Google Photos import keeps its own date. The import writes it and

sentence in a report. The fix that day removed four messaging-app shapes
by name, which left a list of which app writes which kind of filename to

is required, so an eight-digit counter cannot pass.

camera dates on real files: the user's correction, a photo's EXIF, a
video container, a Google import. Weak means it might be a capture time
and might be an arrival time: the filename, and a file mtime.

everything. Either behaviour condemns the group: bunching like a bulk
save (3+ in one minute and over 30% of the set, the same test and number
checkExifSanity already uses, which fits unchanged), or sitting within a
day of its own upload on a day the project's strong-dated photos do not
cover. The video-only 24-hour rule is now this one shared rule.

timelines, openers worked about half the time and closers failed 16 times in
23; one person asked for a specific closing photo and got it at position 58 of
70, after the pipeline had scored it 97 out of 100.

Once the selection is final, one call asks which photo in the first chapter
sets the scene and which in the last feels like an ending. It sees them
together, which a score for each photo on its own cannot do. Two items move;
nothing else about the selection changes.

It will not move a photo it rated below 6, will not end the video on a photo
with no date, will not pick the cover or anything inside a group, and does
nothing at all if the call fails. If the person's own words asked for a
particular opening or ending, that wins and the rating stops applying.

The move is written to both lists that matter, since a chapter with clips
stores its order one way and a photo-only chapter another. Behind one switch
so it can be judged blind.

A chapter's own description reaches its own curator

What someone types per chapter in the Create Timeline modal reached the part
that decides which photos go in which chapter, and stopped there. The part that
picks the actual photos never saw it, except on a one-chapter video where that
path sets the description itself.

Matching them on is not free. The descriptions arrive as a plain ordered list of
strings with no id and no title, so position is the only handle there is, and
the number of chapters the model returns is enforced by a sentence in the prompt
and nothing else. A separate rule merges a two-chapter answer into one, which
can turn four configured chapters into one.

So: match by position when the architect returned exactly the configured number,
counted after that merge, and otherwise pass nothing and warn with the project
and both counts. A description on the wrong chapter is worse than none, because
the curator then picks photos against the wrong brief. The same list decides
which words the opening and ending choice sees for the first and last chapter.

Also: that choice could be told it had followed the person's instructions on a
project where they had written nothing. The claim skips the score bar, so a weak
photo could have been pinned as though it were asked for. It is now refused
unless words were sent, and the model is no longer invited to claim it when
there are none.

The same moment stops shipping twice, behind a switch that is off

When a kept photo and a kept clip show the same moment, the clip stays and the
photo leaves, with its place refilled from the same chapter. Built, tested,
verified by eye, and SWITCHED OFF (SAME_MOMENT_ENABLED = false).

Nothing compared a photo with a clip before. Photos go through embedding
clustering, clips go through nothing equivalent, and the two budgets are filled
independently, so a family swim could ship as a still and as six seconds of video
a few seconds apart.

The rule needs two things together: the photo's time inside the clip's window or
within 120s of either end, AND the pair ranking in the top 0.5% of that project's
own photo-to-clip similarities. Never an absolute cosine (the value at that rank
is 0.80 on one dev project and 0.68 on another) and never ranked against
photo-to-photo similarities (a clip's frame is a soft 320px image). Silent below
500 comparisons, which is most projects, because a rank over 130 comparisons is
not a measurement.

Both sides need a date precise enough to mean it: corrected, EXIF or container,
or a guard-passed filename. Never a file copy time, never a visual estimate.

WHY IT IS OFF. Verified on Outer Banks 2024 at standard (3 pairs, 2 removed) and
Disney World 2018 - 2 at quick (21 pairs, 2 removed, 2 refilled). The rule was
right every time: all four are genuinely one moment. The policy on top of it is
what is unresolved. We pick the clip having seen ONE frame of it, so Outer Banks
dropped a sharp posed shot of a boy and his grandfather holding up a fish for a
motion-blurred frame of the same second. A clip carries motion and sound, a photo
carries composition and sharpness, and the rule sees one of those four things.
Against a yield of one or two photos per project on a third of projects, that is
not a trade to make unlooked-at. To revisit: judge a dozen removals against the
actual clips rather than one frame each, then pick a side from the five options
in the investigation's section 2.4.

Two things found while building it:

Membership in a memory is not a sign the user placed a photo. Apply wraps every
timeline item in a one-photo memory, so on a rebuilt project it covers nearly
every photo (70 memories for 70 items on Outer Banks 2024), and protecting on it
blocked a removal that should have gone through. Protection is now a hand-picked
cover, a photo the user captioned or re-dated, and each chapter's cover nominee.

Every pair found and not acted on logs its reason, and a chapter that ends short
logs what it passed over. "3 found, 0 removed" was how the memory bug hid.

Refilling reuses the top-up's candidate ranking rather than a second copy of it,
plus the extra bars: nothing the curator set aside this run, nothing itself paired
with a kept clip, nothing weaker than the weakest photo the chapter still holds.

title: Fix two stale smoke assertions, the gap one of them found, and a flaky modal test
summary: Two outdated smoke test checks were fixed, and the gap one exposed stops edits recreating deleted photos
detail: The browser smoke test against dev failed two of eleven steps, and both were tests expecting old behaviour: a trailing slash on About, and a project delete that is now done in the background. Chasing the second found that three routes kept serving a project already being deleted. One of them was risky: editing a photo after the delete had removed it would write the row back with no project. One shared check now treats a project being deleted as gone on all of them, while photo deletes stay allowed on purpose. A modal test that finished saving after the test ended was also fixed.
commitMessages:
Fix two stale smoke assertions, and the gap one of them found

The smoke suite is the eleven-step browser check that runs against a deployed
stage. Two of its steps were asserting behaviour that changes on Sep 15 and
Sep 16 replaced, and the suite is manual-dispatch only, so nothing had run it
since Sep 14 to notice.

The About test required the address to end in `/about` and it ends in `/about/`.
That slash is deliberate: prerendered pages are written to <route>/index.html and
the S3 website endpoint redirects the slash-less form, so every internal link,
the sitemap and the canonical tags use the slash. The test now pins the slash, so
a link that drops it fails here instead of quietly costing a redirect.

The delete test read the photo list once, right after the delete, and expected it
empty. Deleting a project stopped being synchronous on Sep 15: the route marks
the project deleting, answers 202, and a worker runs the cascade. The dev worker
logs show it finishing that project in 470ms; the test read the list at about
200ms and got one of the two photos back. It now polls instead of reading once.

Then the gap behind it. Three routes take projectId from the query string, so
checkProjectOwnership cannot run on them, and they checked existence and
ownership but not status. They kept serving a project mid-delete while every
project route already 404'd it. Two are only inconsistent. The third is not:
updatePhoto is a DynamoDB UpdateItem, which creates the item when it is absent,
so an edit landing after the cascade deleted that photo would write the row back
and strand a PHOTO# with no project.

The rule is now one function, isProjectGone in db/projects.js, true for a project
that does not exist and for one whose delete has been accepted. The middleware
uses it and so do GET /api/photos, GET /api/recordings and PUT /api/photos/:id.
The two DELETE routes stay permissive on purpose, and now say why: deleting a
photo out of a project being deleted asks for what the cascade is doing, and
refusing it would break the teardown and sweep paths that rely on it.

One honest cost, written into the test and the changelog: with the 404 in place,
F7 no longer witnesses the cascade finishing, because nothing a browser can see
does once the API hides the project. projectDeletion.test.js and the recorded
bucket checks are what cover that.

Docs: progress.md entry, PARKING_LOT #68 opened and closed, API.md route notes
for both list routes plus its Last verified line.

The two internal callback routes (clip analysis from Cloud Run, render

The callback signing key is re-read every 10 minutes, and rotation keeps old tokens working

Review fixes for the per-job callback tokens (#84). The key used to be cached
for the life of a container, so deleting or rotating it never reached warm
containers and a token minted in one container could fail in another. Now
every container re-reads the key every 10 minutes, whatever the last answer
was, and the verifier accepts the current key or the previous one (the
secret's AWSPREVIOUS version, else the key the container held before). A
failed read keeps the last known keys and waits like any other read, so a
failing Secrets Manager is not called on every request. A secret scheduled
for deletion reads as no key.

The runbook moves into the repo as docs/runbooks/callback-tokens.md, with
the rollback and rotation steps corrected to match.

title: Encrypt stored Google Photos and YouTube tokens (#86)
summary: Stored Google Photos and YouTube tokens are encrypted, and disconnecting now really revokes access
detail: Google tokens that reach a user's photos and channel were stored as plain text on the user record. They are now encrypted with a per-stage key before storage, tied to the user, provider and field so a copied value will not decrypt. The user record no longer carries tokens at all, and one reader decrypts them when needed. Disconnect now revokes with the long-lived token; before, Google refused the usually expired one and the grant stayed live. Merging with account deletion exposed a quiet break, deletion would have stopped revoking Google access, which was fixed and tested. A dry-run migration found 3 connections to encrypt on dev.
commitMessages:
Google Photos and YouTube tokens are encrypted with KMS before they are stored

Tokens on USER# records are written as kms1:<base64>, bound to user, provider
and field, and old plain-text values are still read. getUserById no longer
returns tokens; getUserOAuthTokens is the one read path. A refresh writes only
the new access token, conditioned on the connection still existing. Disconnect
revokes with the refresh token in the POST body. A one-off script encrypts old
records in place. serverless.yml gets a per-stage key ARN (placeholders until
the keys exist), the env var, and kms:Encrypt/Decrypt on that key. PARKING_LOT #86.

commitMessages:
Post-credits photos play after the credits even with section title cards off

The renderer and both timeline builders decided what was post-credits only
from the section title markers, and with cards off there are none, so those
items would have played before the credits (PARKING_LOT #76). An item is now
post-credits when its own section is marked post-credits, answered by one
function, timeline.post_credits_flags, that all three share.

The renderer now takes the full section list, so the timeline rebuilt from
real segment lengths (which the music mix uses) keeps post-credits placement,
section music volume and keep-music-loud with cards off. A crossfaded photo
run is broken where post-credits items begin. With cards on, output is
unchanged (pinned by tests against the old numbers), and the log no longer
says a post-credits section has a card.

The renderer deploys through SSM with one script for laptop and CI

npm run deploy-ec2 now runs backend/src/scripts/deployRenderer.js. It builds
one bundle (the same files the SSH deploy copied, plus a checked-in installer
and the systemd unit), stages it in the stage's videos bucket, and installs it
on the box through SSM Run Command, so no inbound port is needed (#82).

Add Section and Add Post-Credits Section now create the section only when you press Create

the request fails, the dialog stays open with what the user typed.

so the dialog's volume slider takes effect on creation.

title: Renderer keeps uploaded songs: read durationMs, measure the file as a last resort
summary: Uploaded songs stop vanishing from the middle of a music chain
detail: When a section had two songs in a row, an uploaded song that was not the last one disappeared from the video. The renderer only read a track's length from the field library songs use, while uploaded songs store theirs differently, so the length came out as zero and the mixer skipped the song without a word. One helper now reads either field, and a track with no recorded length is measured from the downloaded file. The measuring step was hardened so an unreadable song drops only itself, never the whole render. 327 processing tests pass, and the new ones fail on the old code.
commitMessages:
The renderer plays a user's own music track for its full length in a chain

User music rows store their length as durationMs; the renderer read only
duration (seconds), which library rows have. Every user track reached the
mix with no length, so one followed by another track in its section got a
zero-length slot and the mixer skipped it without a word (PARKING_LOT #114).

One helper, track_duration_ms, now reads durationMs or duration for both
kinds of track. A track whose record has neither is measured from the
downloaded file with ffprobe, and an unmeasurable file is logged by name.
Tests use the real row shapes; the old fixture gave a user row a duration
field real rows never have.

title: Create Timeline crash emails; permissions boundary on the backend Lambda roles
summary: Crashed timeline builds now email the founder, and the backend's cloud roles get a hard permissions ceiling
detail: A Create Timeline run that timed out, ran out of memory or crashed on start used to leave only a bare error with no project id. The worker now sends a 'Background job crashed' email naming the project and step, and AWS no longer retries it, because a rerun would replay up to 15 minutes of paid analysis calls that almost always fail the same way. The same PR put a per-stage permissions boundary on both of the backend's Lambda roles: a ceiling that allows exactly what the live roles use and narrows four grants that could reach the other stage. commitMessages:
A Create Timeline that times out or crashes now emails the founder

The organize worker catches its own errors and emails from its catch block,
but a 15-minute timeout, an out-of-memory kill or a crash while loading never
reaches that block, so those failures showed only as a bare Lambda error with
no project id. aiProducerWorker now has the same onFailure destination as the
other async workers, and asyncWorkerFailure names the job step
(analyze-event or organize-event) next to the project id.

Retries are set to 0: AWS only retries this worker after a timeout, OOM or
start-up crash, and a rerun replays up to 15 minutes of paid Gemini calls that
almost always fail the same way. PARKING_LOT #94.

Cap what CI can grant the backend Lambdas with a per-stage permissions boundary

The CI deploy role must write the stack's IAM roles for serverless deploy, so
any workflow that deploys the backend could give the Lambdas any permission.
Both stack roles (the Lambda role and the custom-resources role, which

title: #84 stage 2: callbacks take only per-job tokens; deleted videos stay deleted
summary: Video callbacks accept only per-job tokens, and deleted videos stop coming back as ghosts
detail: The renderer and the clip analyzer report back to the backend through callbacks that used to accept either a per-job signed token or an old shared password. Both stages had run on tokens alone for over 72 quiet hours, so the password was removed. The one stray password use in that window exposed a real bug: a user deleted a video 4 seconds after queueing it, the renderer retried, and a database write quietly recreated the deleted record and emailed a failure for a video that no longer existed. Seven such ghost records were found. Now every update to a video record, on both the renderer and backend side, only lands if the record still exists, so a deleted video gets no write, no email and no retry.
commitMessages:
Render and clip callbacks accept only per-job tokens; deleted videos stay deleted

Stage 2 of #84. CALLBACK_AUTH=legacy was silent for more than 72 hours in
both stages, so the old shared callback password is no longer accepted or
sent anywhere. verifyCallbackAuth rejects any non-token bearer as
not_a_token. callVideoProcessor and createVideo now refuse a job when no
token can be minted, because such a job could never call back. The six
clip dispatch sites and the renderer no longer read
video-processor-callback-secret, and the renderer sends no callback at
all for a record without a token. Cloud Run is unchanged: it still echoes
the callbackSecret field, which has carried a token since stage one.

The one legacy callback seen during the quiet window was a bug. A user
deleted a dev render 4 seconds after queueing it. The renderer failed on
the missing record three times, and then the attempt cap wrote a stub
VIDEO# record (update_item creates a missing key) and emailed a failure
alert for a deleted video. Seven such stubs exist in dev and prod, some
"complete" from deletes mid-render. Now:
- the renderer drops a job whose record is gone on the first receive;
- every renderer VIDEO# write is conditional on the record existing, and
  a refused write sends no callback (report_render_failure);
- the backend's updateVideoStatus is conditional too, so the stuck-render
  sweep sends no alert for a video deleted under it;
- claimRenderNotification requires createdAt, so an existing stub can
  never send an email.

title: Photo pace (Relaxed / Normal / Fast) and beat timing that lands on the beat
summary: A photo pace setting (Relaxed, Normal, Fast), and photo changes that finally land on the beat
detail: A user wrote in on Oct 1 that photos stayed on screen too long and asked for about one second per photo, and there was no way to change it. Each project now has a photo pace, picked in the Create Video dialog or Settings, with a length estimate for each option. Making the paces line up with music meant rewriting how the renderer times photos: the old beat sync spaced photos like the music but never actually put the changes on the beat. Now every photo lasts a whole number of beats or bars, cuts are placed on the beat grid even after clips and song handovers, and on five test tracks cuts land within 17 ms of a beat. If a faster or slower pace leaves a section short of music, a same-mood track is added and named on screen. The work also fixed four timing bugs nobody had logged, including a fade that never played and cuts drifting up to 6 seconds late over a long section.
commitMessages:

Relaxed, Normal and Fast each carry how long a still photo stays on screen
with and without beat timing, and the seconds length estimates use. The

title: Remove the static from voice recordings in rendered videos
summary: Voice recordings in videos lose the static they had picked up
detail: Every voice recording in a rendered video had audible static. The renderer added a second of silence before each recording by joining a silent clip to the voice, and on the newer FFmpeg that silent clip was 8-bit, so joining them cut the whole voice down to 8 bits. It was saved as 16-bit again afterwards, which hid the problem until the audio was measured step by step. The fix delays the voice by a second instead, so there is only one input and nothing to convert. High-frequency noise dropped back from -39 dB to -75 dB relative to the voice, and a full render of the tribute sample was checked by ear.
commitMessages:
Voice recordings keep their 16-bit sound after the lead-in

The second of silence before each recording came from a lavfi anullsrc
input joined to the voice with concat. FFmpeg 8 decodes that input as
8-bit audio and concat converted the voice to 8 bits too, so every
recording came out with static. The voice is now delayed with adelay
from one input, in a shared prepend_lead_in helper used by both the
single photo and the recorded memory. The new test fails against the
old command (samples off by 255 steps) and passes now.

commitMessages:
Zooms stay gentle on portrait photos and still move on full frames

The founder picked "v1" from test renders of the tribute sample video.
A small face near the top of a portrait photo made the camera slide up
to 27% of the frame while zooming, and photos full of faces barely
zoomed because the close crop could not cut into the padded face box.

Now the crop centre moves at most 6% of the frame (KB_MAX_TRAVEL),
every zoom is at least 6% (KB_MIN_ZOOM), and the close crop may trim
20% off the padded face box (KB_FACE_TRIM). A short Fast photo keeps
its own smaller zoom and its travel cap shrinks with it. Unlike the
prototype, the wide crop's start is chosen inside the photo, so the
cap still holds after it is fitted to the photo edges.

title: Launch gate fixes: account linking, table scans, email and capacity limits
summary: Pre-launch security and capacity fixes: verified-email account linking, email sending limits, and no more whole-table reads
detail: Pre-launch reviews turned up several gaps, each fixed on its own branch, reviewed, then combined. A first Google sign-in now links only to an account whose email is verified, closing a way to take over a stranger's account by putting their email on your own. Photo and recording routes that could read the whole database table to find one item now require a project id and look it up directly. Invitation emails got limits per account, per project and 300 a day for the whole stage, because one abuser could get the shared email account paused and stop every new signup. Only the owner can now record onto a draft memory, every deploy turns on deletion protection for the user pools, photo processing is capped at 50 at a time, and prod's API keeps 200 Lambda slots of its own.
commitMessages:
Google sign-in links only to an account whose email is verified

Security review S1: a signed-in user could put a stranger's email on
their own account without verifying it, and PreSignUp then linked the
stranger's first Google sign-in to that account. A password account now
owns an email only when confirmed, enabled and email_verified is true;
otherwise the Google sign-in becomes its own account, and the unverified
claimant no longer blocks the owner's password signup. setAdmin uses
the same rule.

updateCognitoEmail.js, run after every backend deploy, sent UpdateUserPool
only a few settings, so each deploy reset the rest, including the
email-change verification setting and deletion protection. It now passes
back the whole pool config. The pool setting itself is a by-hand step in
docs/runbooks/cognito-email-verification.md, since the pools are not in
CloudFormation.

Photo and recording routes find the item by key, never by a table scan

Launch-readiness finding S2. GET /api/photos/:id always read the whole
DynamoDB table to find one photo, and PUT/DELETE on /api/photos/:id and
/api/recordings/:id did the same when no project id was sent. Any free
account could loop them to run up the bill and tie up Lambdas.

The five routes now require the project id and answer 400 before any
lookup without it, so the item is one key read and the existing owner
checks apply. GET /api/photos/:id checks the project before reading the
photo. The lightbox side panel, the only caller of the GET, now sends the
project id, and the frontend helpers take it as a required argument.

GET /api/projects/:projectId/recordings is retired: it scanned the table
on every call, always returned an empty list, and nothing called it.

The db helpers' own no-project-id fallbacks are parking lot #144.

Invitation and reminder emails now have daily and hourly limits

Invitations go out through the same SES account that sends Cognito's
sign-up codes, and anyone can unlock invitations for free during the beta.
One person mailing scraped addresses could get SES paused and stop every
new sign-up (launch-readiness security S4).

Each email or text invitation or reminder now takes a slot from the sender
(50 a day, 20 an hour) and from the project (40 a day, 20 an hour), counted
with conditional writes on the USER# and PROJECT# METADATA records. A

title: Create Video renders on Google Cloud Run Jobs, finished videos in GCS
summary: Create Video moves to Google Cloud Run Jobs, one job per video, with the EC2 box as a fallback
detail: Rendering moved off the single EC2 box to Google Cloud Run Jobs, which start one job per video, with finished videos stored in a new Google Cloud Storage bucket. Every place that reads a video, from playback and download to the share page, YouTube upload and deletes, now handles both the old and new storage, so all existing videos keep working. A per-stage switch flips a stage between Cloud Run and EC2 in seconds without a deploy, and the stuck-render sweep now re-sends a lost dispatch once and restarts a stopped box. The renderer stopped calling Rekognition, relying on face data from upload analysis instead, which now uses a fixed answer format plus a repair step for malformed face boxes, and a backfill filled 238 of 238 photos that had lost theirs on dev. The PR also made every email and alert finish sending before a Lambda replies, after two dev renders reached the send but only one email went out.

A renamed or fraction-scaled face box is repaired instead of dropped

The safety net behind the new answer format. normalize_face_box reads x or
left as xmin, y or top as ymin, right as xmax and bottom as ymax, only when
the real key is absent, and moves a corner written as a 0-1 fraction (not a
whole number, strictly between 0 and 1) to the 1000 scale, corner by corner,
since one real box mixed both scales. 0, 1 and anything above 1 stay. Repairs
and drops are counted and logged separately, clamping and dropping are kept.

boxes as faceData. Before this, a group photo whose boxes all said x lost
every face. Tested on the real dev boxes, including the 813a17 box that must
keep xmin 0.

title: 200 MP photos, one photo size limit, Cancel a render, import message, restoration cleanup, email branding
summary: Big phone photos, one 50 MB upload limit, a Cancel button for renders, and brand colors on every email
detail: Six fixes rode together into the same day's prod release. Photos from 200 megapixel phone cameras had been failing completely, 32 of them on prod in one day, and are now accepted up to 268 MP and decoded at reduced size to stay within memory. Uploads got one 50 MB limit everywhere instead of three different ones, and a refused photo's file no longer lingers in storage. A video still being made can be cancelled from the Videos list, which stops the cloud job and uploads nothing. A Google Photos import cut short by the project limit now says how many items came in and why, full-size restoration copies of people's photos are deleted with their photo or project, and all 13 emails moved from black and blue to the app's brown and cream on one shared layout.
commitMessages:
Upload processing handles 200 megapixel photos

Pillow's default decompression-bomb limit (179 MP) refused every photo
from the 200 MP mode of recent Samsung phones, so 32 prod photos failed
with no thumbnail and no analysis. The cap is now a deliberate 268 MP,
just under sharp's limit, so a real bomb is still refused at open.

A large JPEG that must be re-encoded (EXIF orientation, a rotation) is
decoded at the least reduction (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) that fits the Lambda's
1024 MB; measured on a 200 MP photo this drops the peak from 1.7 GB to
0.7 GB. HEIC, PNG and WebP over 64 MP cannot be decoded at reduced scale
and are refused with a clear sentence instead of running out of memory.
Gemini gets the 1,536 px analysis copy when a photo is over 6 MB or
64 MP, since Vertex AI takes at most 7 MB of inline image data. The face
backfill prepares images the same way.

The renderer draws 200 megapixel photos

Every Image.open in the renderer hit Pillow's default 179 MP limit, so a
200 MP photo could not be drawn, and the header read that picks a pan's
direction quietly gave up. The renderer now sets the same 268 MP cap as
upload processing, in video/image_limits.py.

Nothing is rendered above 4K, so a downloaded photo over 5120 px on the
long edge is replaced, once, by a 5120 px copy, decoded at reduced scale
for JPEG. Every later reader sees the small file: the Ken Burns loaders,
ffprobe's check, the pan check and the title cards' page for Chromium.
The tests decode a real 200 MP JPEG in a separate process, since
conftest mocks Pillow for the rest of the suite.

A photo whose upload processing failed stayed failed forever: nothing

title: Cancelled-render tests run in their own temp folder, so the dev deploy's image check passes
summary: Test fix unblocks the dev deploy of the previous day's bundle
detail: The dev deploy of the six-fix bundle stopped at the renderer image check. Four new tests had let the render's download step create a temp folder inside the checkout, which the image check mounts read-only. They passed on the laptop and in CI, where the folder is writable, so the frontend deployed but the renderer job, EC2 box and backend were held back. The tests now use their own temp folder, and the full suite of 1,465 tests passed inside the image the same way the deploy runs it.
commitMessages:
Cancelled-render tests run in their own temp folder, so the image check passes

The deploy's image check mounts the checkout read-only, and these tests let
the render's download step create a relative ./temp folder there. They passed
on the laptop and in CI, where the folder is writable, and failed the dev
deploy of #255. Run from tmp_path and point TEMP_DIR into it.

title: Redesign the title slide themes and keep titles off faces
summary: Title slide themes redesigned into 12 distinct looks, with titles that stay off people's faces
detail: The theme picker now offers 12 themes that look clearly different from each other. Cinematic is new, three themes were reworked and renamed (Postcard, Linen and Soft Light), and two were retired, with projects that used them moved to the closest remaining theme. Title slides now lay themselves out: the photo is cropped around the faces, titles size to their space, and full-photo themes place the words where they touch no face, falling back to a side-panel layout. The renderer passes face boxes to the title slide, and the picker preview runs the same layout script on the same data, so what users see is what renders.
commitMessages:
Redesign the title slide themes and keep titles off faces

The picker now has 12 themes that look clearly different from each other.
Cinematic is new; Ocean Breeze becomes Postcard, Gentle Farewell becomes
Linen and Eternal Light becomes Soft Light; the Tribute tab is labelled
Quiet & Reflective. Champagne Toast and Vintage Sepia leave the picker, and
projects that chose them resolve to Gatsby Gold and Photo Album.

Title slides lay themselves out in the page (templates/_shared/layout.js):
the photo is cropped around the faces, titles size to their space, and the
full-photo themes place the words where they touch no face, falling back to
a side panel layout. The renderer passes face boxes from title_photo_layout,
the out-of-timeline cover now carries faceData and cameraHints, and the
picker preview runs the same script on the same data.
